questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. What an ongoing role adds
questions.question: A Senegalese telecom's board makes its chief audit executive permanently responsible for the data privacy office. Which step do the Standards require MOST specifically because the role is ongoing?

options.A: Set a plan to hand the role back to management
options.B: Keep third-party assurance until 12 months after the role ends
options.C: Write the role and its safeguards into the internal audit charter
options.D: Advise the board and senior management on suitable safeguards

questions.key_concept: An ongoing role beyond internal auditing must be written into the charter: its responsibilities, the nature of the work and the safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four steps into three piles: any such role, a temporary role, an ongoing role.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 separates two cases. For a role beyond internal auditing that continues, the chief audit executive must write the responsibilities, the nature of the work and the safeguards into the internal audit charter, which the board approves. Advising the board and senior management on safeguards, the closest choice, is required for every such role, whatever its length. The hand-back plan and the 12 months after the role ends belong to a temporary role.

wrong_explanations.A: A plan to return the duties to management is required when the role is temporary. This role is permanent, so there is nothing to hand back.
wrong_explanations.B: Another route to assurance is needed here too, but the 12 months after the role ends is the temporary-role rule. An ongoing role has no end date.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: advice on safeguards is a must here too, but for any role that could impair independence, temporary or ongoing. It is not what the role's length adds.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a hand-back plan belongs to a temporary role, and B, because assurance until 12 months after the end is also a temporary-role rule.
Final two: C beats D because advice on safeguards is required for every role beyond internal auditing; the step tied to an ongoing role is recording it in the charter.
Exam cue: for a role beyond internal auditing, read the duration first. Ongoing: charter and another route to assurance. Temporary: third-party assurance, 12 months after, and a hand-back plan.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Declining to rely on second-line work
questions.question: A Kenyan mobile-money firm's finance director wants internal audit to rely on compliance's agent-monitoring tests, which covered five of 900 agents and left nothing on file. What is the chief audit executive's BEST course?

options.A: Decline to rely on the tests and have internal auditors retest
options.B: Rely on the tests and document the basis for doing so
options.C: Rely on the tests and leave their conclusions with compliance
options.D: Raise the lack of coordination with senior management, then the board

questions.key_concept: Reliance is the chief audit executive's choice, made after evaluating the other provider's work. Work too weak to support conclusions is retested or redone.
questions.pre_read: A basis for reliance has to exist before it can be documented. Would these tests support a conclusion on 900 agents?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.5 asks the chief audit executive to consider relying on other providers, not to rely on them, and leaves that executive responsible for internal audit's conclusions. Its considerations add that, after evaluating the work, the chief audit executive may decide it cannot be relied on; internal auditors then retest or do the work themselves. Documenting a basis, the closest choice, is the rule when reliance is justified. Here there is none.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a documented basis is required when internal audit relies on another provider. Five agents out of 900, with nothing kept on file, give no sound basis to record.
wrong_explanations.C: Responsibility for internal audit's conclusions stays with the chief audit executive, whoever's work they rest on. It cannot be passed to compliance.
wrong_explanations.D: A coordination concern is raised with senior management first, then the board if needed, once coordination proves out of reach. The issue here is the quality of the work.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the chief audit executive stays responsible for internal audit's conclusions, and D, because the problem is weak testing, not a failure to coordinate.
Final two: A beats B because a basis must exist before it is documented; tests of five agents with nothing on file are retested, not relied on.
Exam cue: coordinate with every assurance provider, but rely only after evaluating the work. Saving effort is a reason to consider reliance; only work that holds up is a basis for it.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Whose follow-up is it
questions.question: The three-person internal audit function of a Norwegian fish farm is offered four standing tasks. Which task would MOST clearly be a second-line duty that could impair its independence?

options.A: Reviewing management's risk register when updating its own audit universe
options.B: Running the follow-up of actions from management's risk reviews
options.C: Consolidating the assurance providers' results into one report for the board
options.D: Running the follow-up of actions from its own engagements

questions.key_concept: Internal audit follows up actions from its own engagements. By The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management, it must not own management's follow-up.
questions.pre_read: Two options look alike. For each task, ask whose actions are being chased and who would answer if they slipped.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management draws the line by ownership. Internal audit monitors whether actions agreed in its own engagements are carried out, keeps its audit universe and brings assurance results together; all three serve its own planning and reporting. Chasing the actions from management's risk reviews is management's follow-up, which the statement says internal audit must not own. Following up its own engagements, the closest choice, is what Standard 15.2 requires.

wrong_explanations.A: Using management's risk information to keep its own audit universe current is part of planning internal audit's work. Internal audit reads the register; it does not run it.
wrong_explanations.C: The statement lists coordinating and consolidating assurance results among internal audit's own activities. It gives the board one picture without owning anyone's controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it looks the same, but these actions come from internal audit's own engagements. Confirming they were implemented is required by Standard 15.2.

tips: Eliminate: A, because reading management's risk register to update the audit universe serves internal audit's own planning, and C, because consolidating assurance results is listed among internal audit's own activities.
Final two: B beats D because internal audit confirms actions from its own engagements, while actions from management's risk reviews are management's to follow up.
Exam cue: when two tasks look alike, ask who owns the process. Internal audit may track its own results; running management's tracking makes it part of what it audits.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. What conformance is measured against
questions.question: Internal auditor Petra finds that a Slovak rail operator's internal audit function meets every requirement of a standard but skips a practice in its considerations for implementation. How should Petra BEST treat the skipped practice?

options.A: As nonconformance to disclose in each final engagement communication
options.B: As an essential condition the board may agree to set aside
options.C: As a preferred practice that conformance does not depend on
options.D: As a departure the chief audit executive must document and explain

questions.key_concept: Conformance is measured against a standard's requirements. Considerations for implementation describe preferred or optional practice, so skipping one needs no documented departure.
questions.pre_read: Which part of a standard uses 'must', and which uses 'should' or 'may'? Decide that before judging the gap.
questions.correct_explanation: Each standard has requirements, which use 'must', and considerations for implementation, which use 'should' for preferred practice and 'may' for optional practice. The function meets every requirement, so it conforms and the skipped practice calls for nothing more. Documenting and explaining a departure, the closest choice, is what Standard 4.1 asks of the chief audit executive when a requirement cannot be met. No requirement is unmet here.

wrong_explanations.A: A final communication discloses nonconformance when an engagement was not carried out in line with the Standards. Skipping a preferred practice is not nonconformance.
wrong_explanations.B: Essential conditions are the board's and senior management's part in Domain III. Agreeing that one is unnecessary applies to those, not to a preferred practice in the considerations.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: when a requirement cannot be met, the chief audit executive records and reports what happened, what was done instead, its effect and why. Every requirement is met here.

tips: Eliminate: A, because disclosure in a final communication is for an engagement that did not conform, and B, because setting a condition aside by agreement applies to essential conditions.
Final two: C beats D because documenting a departure is required when a requirement cannot be met; a skipped 'should' or 'may' leaves conformance intact.

Exam cue: check which part of the standard the practice sits in. Requirements bind; considerations describe preferred or optional practice; essential conditions belong to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. A rating scheme and the conditions for effectiveness
questions.question: A Moroccan retailer's chief audit executive bases internal auditors' yearly performance ratings mainly on satisfaction scores from the managers they audit. Which condition for effective internal auditing does this MOST directly threaten?

options.A: Internal auditors free from undue influence in their assessments
options.B: A function positioned independently, with accountability to the board
options.C: Internal auditors with the competencies the work needs
options.D: Unrestricted access to records, personnel and physical property

questions.key_concept: Effective internal auditing needs auditors free from undue influence. Ratings that depend on the managers they audit threaten that, whatever the reporting line.
questions.pre_read: Has anything changed about where the function sits, or about what could sway each auditor's judgment?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain I ties effective internal auditing to three conditions; the third is internal auditors who are free from undue influence and judge objectively. Ratings that depend mainly on the managers under review give each auditor a reason to please them, and Standard 2.2's considerations name that arrangement as a possible impairment of objectivity. Positioning, the closest choice, is about the function's reporting line, which the rating scheme leaves as it was.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: independence is about where the function sits and whom it answers to. The chief audit executive's own rating scheme changes neither; it works on each auditor's judgment.
wrong_explanations.C: Competence is a separate condition. Nothing in the facts suggests the auditors lack knowledge or skill; the scheme works on their motives.
wrong_explanations.D: Access to records, people and property comes with the function's authority. No access has been restricted, and access is not one of Domain I's three conditions.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the scheme changes motives and not skills, and D, because access is part of the function's authority and has not been restricted.
Final two: A beats B because the scheme leaves the function's position untouched; it gives each auditor a reason to please managers, which is objectivity, a matter of the person.
Exam cue: ask what the fact changes. A reporting line or an outside restriction touches independence; a personal interest, tie or reward touches an auditor's objectivity.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. Which required part settles a dispute
questions.question: A division head at an Ethiopian flower exporter calls internal audit just a unit of the finance department. Which required part of the charter should internal auditor Selam cite to settle this MOST directly?

options.A: The Purpose of Internal Auditing
options.B: The commitment to follow the Standards
options.C: The mandate, with its authority, role and responsibilities
options.D: The organizational position and reporting relationships

questions.key_concept: The charter must state the function's organizational position and reporting relationships, as the board has determined them. That part says where the function sits.
questions.pre_read: List the four things every charter must state. Which one says where the function sits in the organization?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 has the charter state at least four things: the Purpose of Internal Auditing, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate, and the function's organizational position and reporting relationships. Standard 7.1 adds that the board determines that position and the chief audit executive records it in the charter, which settles whether the function belongs to finance. The mandate, the closest choice, says what the function is empowered to do, not where it sits.

wrong_explanations.A: The purpose section says why internal auditing exists and what it gives the board and management. It does not place the function in the structure.
wrong_explanations.B: The commitment to the Standards binds the function to professional requirements. It would matter in a dispute about how the work is done, not about where the function sits.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the mandate gives authority, role and responsibilities. That authority flows from the reporting line, but the line itself is recorded under position and reporting relationships.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the purpose states why internal auditing exists, and B, because the commitment to the Standards concerns how the work is done.
Final two: D beats C because the mandate says what the function is empowered to do, while position and reporting relationships say where it sits and to whom it answers.
Exam cue: match the dispute to the charter part. Why we exist: purpose. How we work: the Standards. What we may do: the mandate. Where we sit: position and reporting relationships.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. The discussion still missing before the vote
questions.question: A Sri Lankan tea broker's audit committee has discussed chief audit executive Nimali's proposed charter and votes next week; the chief executive and finance director have not seen it. What should Nimali do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the chief executive to approve the proposed charter
options.B: Discuss the proposed charter with senior management
options.C: Present the final draft to the audit committee for approval
options.D: Send senior management the proposed charter for information

questions.key_concept: Before approval, the chief audit executive must discuss a proposed charter with the board and senior management. Senior management gives input and does not approve.
questions.pre_read: Two groups must hear the proposed charter before anyone votes. Which group has not been heard yet?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 6.2 a proposed charter is talked through with senior management as well as the board before approval, so the text matches what each group understands and expects of the function. The committee has had its discussion; the executives have not, so theirs comes first. Sending them the text for information, the closest choice, lets them see it but invites no input. Senior management gives input; approval stays with the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Senior management discusses the proposed charter and gives input. Approval is the board's; an executive approves a charter where that person acts as the governing body.
wrong_explanations.C: A final draft usually goes to a board meeting for approval, but that step follows senior management's discussion of the proposed text, which has not happened.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the executives would see the text, but the requirement is a discussion that confirms it reflects what they understand and expect. Information alone gathers no input.

tips: Eliminate: A, because senior management gives input and does not approve the charter, and C, because the final draft goes for approval after both groups have discussed it.
Final two: B beats D because the requirement is a discussion that draws out senior management's expectations; sending the text for information tells them without hearing them.
Exam cue: for the charter, think 'discuss with two, approve by one'. Check that the board and senior management have each discussed the text before the board votes.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. Work that waits for a charter amendment
questions.question: A Ghanaian brewery's internal audit charter lists assurance services only; the board considers chief audit executive Abla's amendment adding advisory services next month. How should Abla BEST answer a manager who wants advisory work now?

options.A: Accept the request, and cover the work in routine board reporting
options.B: Hold the request until the board has approved the amended charter
options.C: Accept the request once the manager has agreed its nature and scope
options.D: Hold the request until the team has the skills the work needs

questions.key_concept: The charter's types of services are approved by the board. Until the board approves an amendment, a service the charter does not list waits.
questions.pre_read: What does the charter list today, and who decides when that list changes?
questions.correct_explanation: The function's authority comes from its mandate. Standard 6.2 has the charter state it, with the kinds of service the function provides, and under Standard 6.1 the charter is the board's to approve. This charter lists assurance only, so advisory work lies outside what the board has authorized until it approves the amendment. Accepting and reporting later, the closest choice, fits a charter that already covers advisory services.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: where the charter already covers advisory services, the work is simply reported to the board. Here advisory work is not yet among the services the board has approved.
wrong_explanations.C: Agreement with the manager shapes the nature and scope of one advisory engagement. It cannot add a type of service to a charter that the board approves.
wrong_explanations.D: Right where the internal auditors lack the competencies a requested service needs. The stem reports no such gap; what is missing is the board's approval of advisory services.

tips: Eliminate: C, because agreeing scope with a manager shapes one engagement and not the charter's services, and D, because the stem reports no skills gap in the team.
Final two: B beats A because routine reporting is enough when the charter already covers advisory work; here the board has not yet approved that type of service.
Exam cue: before asking how advisory work is agreed or reported, check that the charter covers it. Types of services are board-approved content, and so is any change to them.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A request labeled advisory
questions.question: An Estonian bank's treasury head asks internal audit for light advisory work ending in a letter to the board stating that treasury controls are effective. How should internal auditor Maarja BEST classify the request?

options.A: Advisory: its nature and scope are agreed with the treasury head
options.B: Advisory: light work cannot support a conclusion on treasury controls
options.C: Assurance: the letter is addressed to the board
options.D: Assurance: the letter gives a conclusion on control effectiveness

questions.key_concept: The deliverable decides the service. A statement that controls are effective is assurance; advisory work gives advice and no assurance, whatever the request is called.
questions.pre_read: Look past the label on the request. What will the letter tell its reader, and would the reader rely on it?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary treats assurance as a statement meant to raise confidence in how something is governed and controlled, measured against criteria, and advisory services as advice without assurance. A letter telling the board that treasury controls are effective is such a statement, so the work must be planned as assurance. Agreeing scope with the requester, the closest choice, is how advisory work is set up; it cannot turn a conclusion on effectiveness into advice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: advisory nature and scope are agreed with the requester, but the requested letter gives assurance. How the scope is settled does not change that.
wrong_explanations.B: How much work is done affects the level of assurance, not the type of service. A requested statement that controls are effective is assurance, however light the work.
wrong_explanations.C: The letter does go to the board, but who receives a result does not classify the work. Advice can reach the board too; what the letter states decides.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the amount of work affects the level of assurance and not the type of service, and C, because who receives the letter does not decide the type.
Final two: D beats A because advisory work gives no assurance; a letter concluding that controls are effective is assurance, however its scope was agreed.
Exam cue: classify by what is delivered, not by the label, the requester or the reader. A conclusion against criteria is assurance; ideas and input are advice.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. What an advisory agreement cannot waive
questions.question: A Japanese paper mill's plant manager wants informal comments on a draft maintenance procedure, and internal auditor Kaito agrees to keep the work as light as the Standards allow. Which step remains MOST clearly required?

options.A: Approval of the objectives and scope by the chief audit executive
options.B: A formal, documented assessment of the procedure's risks
options.C: Identification of criteria to evaluate the procedure against
options.D: Confirmation of objectivity by the chief audit executive

questions.key_concept: By agreement, advisory work may drop a formal risk assessment, criteria and evidence-based findings. Approval of objectives and scope by the chief audit executive remains.
questions.pre_read: Some steps carry an advisory exception in the Standards, and one arises only before later assurance. Which listed step is neither?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards apply to advisory work unless a standard says otherwise, and three say so: depending on the agreement, a formal documented risk assessment (Standard 13.2), evaluation criteria (Standard 13.4) and evidence gathered to develop findings (Standard 14.2) may not be needed. Standard 13.3 has no such exception, so the chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, still approves the objectives and scope. The formal risk assessment, the closest choice, is required for assurance work.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: assurance work needs a documented risk assessment. For advisory work Standard 13.2 lets a formal, documented one be left out by agreement; understanding the activity stays.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 13.4 says criteria may not be necessary for advisory services, depending on the agreement. Standard 13.6 only has a work program list the criteria that will be used.
wrong_explanations.D: That confirmation is required when assurance is to follow advisory work in the same area. The facts describe advisory comments only.

tips: Eliminate: C, because criteria may be left out of advisory work by agreement, and D, because the objectivity confirmation is for assurance that follows advisory work.
Final two: A beats B because Standard 13.2 excuses a formal, documented risk assessment in advisory work, while Standard 13.3 excuses no engagement from approval of its objectives and scope.
Exam cue: by agreement, advisory work may drop three things: the formal risk assessment, criteria, and evidence gathered for findings. Approval of objectives and scope is never one of them.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A significant risk met in advisory work
questions.question: Mapping a Durban retailer's refund process under an advisory agreement that excludes findings, internal auditor Thabo determines that one clerk who both approves and pays refunds poses a significant risk. What is Thabo's BEST course?

options.A: Document the risk, and keep it to the engagement file
options.B: Document the risk, and hold it until assurance work can test it
options.C: Communicate it as an engagement finding, and place the risk on record
options.D: Stop the mapping, and convert the work to an assurance engagement

questions.key_concept: A significant risk has to be written up and reported as a finding. An advisory agreement can waive gathering evidence for findings, not that duty.
questions.pre_read: The agreement limits what Thabo sets out to look for. Does it also limit what Thabo must do with a significant risk already seen?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2 lets an advisory agreement dispense with gathering evidence to develop findings. It does not touch Standard 14.3: once internal auditors determine that the organization faces a significant risk, they record and report it as a finding, and Standard 1.1 forbids leaving pertinent information out. Holding it until assurance work tests it, the closest choice, documents the risk but leaves it unreported. The agreed terms shape the work, not what must be disclosed.

wrong_explanations.A: A record in the file meets half the duty. A significant risk must also be communicated as a finding; the agreement cannot keep it inside the workpapers.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: more testing would add evidence, but Thabo has already determined the risk is significant. From that point Standard 14.3 has it communicated as a finding, not held back.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing the type of engagement is not Thabo's call alone: changes to objectives and scope need the chief audit executive's approval. Reporting the risk needs no conversion.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a significant risk kept in the file is documented but not communicated, and D, because converting the engagement needs the chief audit executive's approval and is not needed to report.
Final two: C beats B because the risk is already determined; holding it for later testing leaves it unreported, and Standard 14.3 has no exception for advisory work.
Exam cue: an advisory agreement can narrow what you look for, not what you must report. A significant risk you have determined is documented and communicated.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A request to swap assurance for advice
questions.question: A Hungarian logistics firm's operations director asks chief audit executive Eszter to replace the planned warehouse-safety assurance engagement with advice on a safety redesign; the charter covers both services. What must Eszter MOST clearly do?

options.A: Approve the swap as a change to the engagement's objectives and scope
options.B: Discuss with the board and senior management whether the mandate still fits
options.C: Put the director's request before the board and senior management
options.D: Agree the nature and scope of the advice with the director

questions.key_concept: Replacing planned assurance with advisory work is a conflicting demand. The board and senior management must hear of it from the chief audit executive.
questions.pre_read: The director is asking for more than advice: an engagement in the approved plan would disappear. Who needs to hear about that?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 names this case. The chief audit executive must tell the board and senior management in good time of conflicting demands for services, and one example it gives is a request to swap a planned assurance engagement for an advisory one. The board approved the plan and would lose assurance on warehouse safety. Agreeing the advice with the director, the closest choice, suits an ordinary advisory request, not one that displaces planned assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: The chief audit executive approves objectives and scope inside an engagement. Replacing an engagement in the plan is a plan matter that the board and senior management must hear.
wrong_explanations.B: A mandate discussion follows a change in circumstances that may outgrow the charter. This charter already covers both services, and one request does not put the mandate in question.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: advisory nature and scope are agreed with the requester, but this request also removes a planned assurance engagement, which is not the director's to settle.

tips: Eliminate: A, because swapping a planned engagement is a plan matter and not a change of scope inside one engagement, and B, because the charter already covers both services.
Final two: C beats D because the request displaces assurance in the approved plan; Standard 9.4 makes that a conflicting demand to put before the board and senior management.
Exam cue: an advisory request that adds work is agreed with the requester. One that replaces planned assurance is a conflicting demand for the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. Criteria for a contract compliance audit
questions.question: A Kenyan tea packer's board suspects its freight carrier of overbilling and late deliveries and asks for an assurance engagement. Which criteria BEST fit internal auditor Achieng's assessment of the carrier's invoices and deliveries?

options.A: The rates and delivery windows in the freight contract
options.B: The freight rates and delivery times in this year's budget
options.C: The delivery windows the packer promises its own customers
options.D: The rates and delivery times rival carriers quoted

questions.key_concept: Compliance includes keeping to contracts. In a contract compliance audit the agreed terms are the criteria; budgets and market rates answer other questions.
questions.pre_read: 'Overbilling' and 'late' compared with what? Name the document that says what the carrier promised.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary counts contracts among the requirements that compliance means keeping to, and Standard 13.4's considerations list contractual obligations as external criteria. Whether the carrier overbilled or delivered late can be judged against the rates and delivery windows it agreed to, which makes this a contract compliance audit. Rival carriers' quotes, the closest choice, would show whether the deal is competitive, not whether its terms were kept.

wrong_explanations.B: A budget is the packer's own forecast of freight cost and timing. Spending above it is a variance to explain, not proof the carrier billed more than agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: What the packer promises its customers binds the packer. The carrier is late when it misses the windows it accepted in its own contract.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: quotes from rival carriers show whether the terms are competitive. Overbilling and lateness are measured against what this carrier agreed to.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a budget is the packer's own forecast and not the carrier's obligation, and C, because promises to customers bind the packer, not the carrier.
Final two: A beats D because overbilling and lateness mean departing from agreed terms; rival carriers' quotes show competitiveness, a different question.
Exam cue: name the criteria from the question asked. Kept its promises: the contract. Stayed on plan: the budget. Good value: a benchmark.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A Topical Requirement in assurance and advisory work
questions.question: A Latvian insurer's internal audit plan includes advisory work on a draft cybersecurity policy; mid-year the board adds an assurance engagement on the payment unit's cybersecurity. How does the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement MOST accurately apply?

options.A: Mandatory for both the policy work and the payment-unit work
options.B: Mandatory for the policy work; recommended for the payment-unit work
options.C: Mandatory for the payment-unit work; not applicable to the policy work
options.D: Mandatory for the payment-unit work; recommended for the policy work

questions.key_concept: Assurance work on a Topical Requirement's subject has to conform with it; for advisory work, conforming is recommended. Being planned or added later changes nothing.
questions.pre_read: Two things differ between the engagements: the type of service and whether it was planned. Which one sets the Topical Requirement's force?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards say only that internal auditors must conform with a Topical Requirement when an engagement's scope takes in its topic. The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement and the application guidance then set the force: assurance work has to conform, each requirement being assessed for applicability, and for advisory work conforming is recommended. A request outside the original plan is covered too. 'Not applicable', the closest choice, goes too far for advisory work on the topic.

wrong_explanations.A: The Standards' own sentence says to conform when the topic is in scope, but the Topical Requirement sets the force: recommended, not mandatory, for advisory services.
wrong_explanations.B: Timing does not decide. A request outside the original plan is one of the three cases in which a Topical Requirement applies, so the added assurance engagement must conform.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the assurance half is right, but a Topical Requirement is not switched off for advisory work on its topic. Following it there is recommended.

tips: Eliminate: A, because conformance is recommended and not mandatory for advisory services, and B, because an assurance engagement added after the plan was set is still covered.
Final two: D beats C because advisory work on the topic is not exempt; the Topical Requirement is recommended there, and mandatory for the assurance engagement.
Exam cue: for a Topical Requirement, ask what kind of service it is, not when the work was planned. Assurance: must conform. Advisory: recommended.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. The objective of an audit of culture
questions.question: After crews hid two near-misses, the board of a Greek ferry line asks its internal audit function for an assurance engagement on safety culture. Which engagement objective fits that request BEST?

options.A: To assess how near-misses are recorded, reported and followed up
options.B: To assess how expected safety behavior is set, encouraged and monitored
options.C: To assess how safety training is designed, delivered and kept current
options.D: To assess how crew satisfaction is surveyed, analyzed and acted on

questions.key_concept: An audit of culture assesses the governance, risk management and control processes that shape behavior. One reporting process, training or a survey is a part.
questions.pre_read: Assurance is always about governance, risk management and control processes over a subject. What would those be when the subject is behavior?
questions.correct_explanation: By the glossary, assurance concerns the governance, risk management and control processes over a subject, compared with criteria. When the subject is culture, those processes are how leaders set the behavior they expect, encourage it and check on it; Standard 9.1 treats promoting an ethical culture as part of governance, and Standard 1.2's considerations trace such a culture to codes, policies and values. The near-miss process, the closest choice, is one symptom of it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: near-miss reporting is the symptom the board saw. An engagement limited to it would not show why crews chose to hide events, which is the culture question.
wrong_explanations.C: Training is one of the controls that shape behavior. An engagement limited to it would not show how expected behavior is encouraged or checked.
wrong_explanations.D: Satisfaction is how crews feel about their work, not how they behave. Survey results may inform a culture engagement; they are not its subject.

tips: Eliminate: C, because training is one control among those that shape behavior, and D, because satisfaction is not the same thing as behavior.

Final two: B beats A because the board asked about culture; the near-miss process is where the problem showed, while a culture engagement covers how expected behavior is set, encouraged and monitored.

Exam cue: for any assurance engagement, name the subject, then ask what governance, risk management and control processes sit over it. For culture: how the organization sets, promotes and checks expected conduct.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. An audit of the management reporting process
questions.question: A Chilean courier firm's board pack shows 97% on-time delivery, yet customer complaints about lateness keep rising. Which internal audit engagement would MOST directly tell the board whether it can rely on the pack's figure?

options.A: A compliance audit of delivery terms in customer contracts
options.B: An operational audit of the delivery process
options.C: An audit of the firm's management reporting process
options.D: A financial audit of delivery revenue and costs

questions.key_concept: When the board asks whether a reported figure can be relied on, the engagement that fits is an audit of the management reporting process.
questions.pre_read: Is the board asking why deliveries are late, or whether the number it was given can be trusted?
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question is about the figure, not the deliveries. The Part 1 syllabus lists audits of the management reporting process among assurance engagements, Standard 9.1 names reliable financial and operational information as a key risk area, and Standard 13.3's considerations count reporting accurate, reliable information among what assurance covers. An operational audit, the closest choice, would show how well deliveries run, not whether the pack's 97% can be relied on.

wrong_explanations.A: A contract compliance audit tests whether agreed terms were kept. It could find late deliveries, but its subject is the contracts, not the figure the board is given.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an operational audit assesses how effectively and efficiently deliveries run. It would explain lateness, not whether the reported figure is reliable.
wrong_explanations.D: A financial audit looks at financial information and the controls behind it. On-time delivery is operational information, and its reporting is the question here.

tips: Eliminate: A, because contract terms are a different yardstick from the reported figure, and D, because on-time delivery is operational and not financial information.
Final two: C beats B because the board asked whether it can rely on the figure; an operational audit explains delivery performance, which is a different question.
Exam cue: name the engagement from the question the board asks. How well does it run: operational. Was a rule kept: compliance. Can we trust the report: management reporting.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. Internal audit's financial work and the external opinion
questions.question: A Mongolian cashmere exporter's lenders require accounts carrying an independent opinion they can rely on; its internal audit function audits revenue reporting for the board. Whose work do the lenders' terms MOST clearly call for?

options.A: The external auditor's, engaged to report on the full statements
options.B: The internal audit function's, with its report sent to the lenders
options.C: The finance function's, with the finance director's sign-off
options.D: The audit committee's, as the body overseeing financial reporting

questions.key_concept: Internal audit's financial work gives the board and management assurance. An independent opinion on the accounts for outside parties comes from the external auditor.
questions.pre_read: Who is the opinion written for: people inside the organization, or people outside it?
questions.correct_explanation: By the Purpose of Internal Auditing the function serves the board and management. The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model places external audit outside the three lines: it gives an independent opinion, usually on the financial statements, to creditors and other outside stakeholders. Lenders ask for that. Sending them internal audit's report, the closest choice, changes its readers, not what it covers or whom it was written for.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Standard 11.3 lets results go outside the organization after due advice, but this report covers revenue for the board. Lenders want an opinion on the accounts.
wrong_explanations.C: Finance prepares the accounts and its director signs them as management. That sign-off is management's own statement, not an independent opinion on it.
wrong_explanations.D: An audit committee oversees; it does not perform audit work or issue an opinion on the accounts. The lenders want the work of an independent auditor.

tips: Eliminate: C, because finance cannot give an independent opinion on accounts it prepares, and D, because the audit committee oversees audit work and does not perform it.
Final two: A beats B because the lenders want an independent opinion on the accounts; internal audit's report covers revenue for the board, whoever reads it.
Exam cue: ask who relies on the work. The board and management: internal audit. Lenders, regulators or other outside parties: the external auditor's opinion.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Recognizing internal benchmarking
questions.question: A Vietnamese furniture maker's operations head asks internal audit, as advisory work, why its plants scrap so much timber. Which analysis by internal auditor Khanh would MOST accurately be called internal benchmarking?

options.A: Comparing scrap rates with the target in the production plan
options.B: Comparing this year's scrap rates with last year's
options.C: Comparing scrap rates with those of other furniture makers
options.D: Comparing scrap rates across the maker's three plants

questions.key_concept: Internal benchmarking compares the same measure between areas of one organization. Comparing with similar organizations is external benchmarking; management decides what to change.
questions.pre_read: Benchmarking needs a comparison partner. For the internal kind, where does that partner sit?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.2's considerations list internal benchmarking, a comparison between areas of the same organization, and external benchmarking, a comparison with similar organizations, as separate analyses. Setting the three plants' scrap rates side by side is the internal kind. Comparing with other furniture makers, the closest choice, is benchmarking too, but the external kind. Either way the auditor explains the differences and management decides what to change.

wrong_explanations.A: Comparing results with a target sets the condition against criteria. That is how a gap is found, not benchmarking between areas.
wrong_explanations.B: Comparing a measure with the same measure in an earlier period is a trend comparison. The partner is the past, not another area.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: this is benchmarking, but against similar organizations, which makes it external. The internal kind stays inside one organization.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a comparison with a target sets condition against criteria, and B, because a comparison with last year is a trend analysis.
Final two: D beats C because internal benchmarking compares areas inside one organization; comparing with other makers is external benchmarking.
Exam cue: name a comparison by its partner. Another unit: internal benchmarking. Another organization: external benchmarking. An earlier period: trend. A target: criteria.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Advisory work the internal auditors start
questions.question: A Peruvian fishing cooperative's internal audit charter covers advisory services, and chief audit executive Milagros believes mapping the catch-payment process would help its manager, who has not asked. What is Milagros's BEST course?

options.A: Hold the idea until the manager or the board requests it
options.B: Propose an assurance engagement, and agree its scope with the manager
options.C: Propose the mapping to the manager, and agree on its scope
options.D: Seek the board's approval before raising the idea with the manager

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors may start advisory work themselves; it need not wait for a request. Its nature and scope are still agreed with the stakeholders concerned.
questions.pre_read: Must advisory work begin with someone else's request? And once begun, who has to agree what it will cover?
questions.correct_explanation: The introduction to Domain V says internal auditors may initiate advisory services as well as perform them on request, and the glossary makes their nature and scope a matter of agreement with the stakeholders concerned. So Milagros can put the idea to the manager and settle with them what the mapping will cover. Waiting for a request, the closest choice, treats advisory work as something others have to start; the Standards do not.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: many advisory engagements do start with a request, but the Standards also let internal auditors initiate them. Nothing requires waiting to be asked.
wrong_explanations.B: The manager needs help seeing the process, not a conclusion against criteria. And an assurance engagement's scope is set mainly by the internal auditors, not agreed with the manager.
wrong_explanations.D: The board approves the plan and significant changes to it. Nothing requires its approval before an idea for advisory work is raised with the manager concerned.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the need is advice and an assurance scope is not agreed with the manager, and D, because board approval is for the plan and significant changes, not for raising an idea.
Final two: C beats A because internal auditors may initiate advisory services themselves; they still agree the nature and scope with the manager before starting.
Exam cue: advisory work can start from either side. Either way, its nature and scope are agreed with the stakeholders concerned, and every decision stays with management.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Taking part in due diligence
questions.question: The chief executive of a Bangladeshi food group asks its internal audit function to take part in due diligence on a planned purchase of a rival. Which description of the function's part is MOST accurate?

options.A: Assurance: it concludes whether the rival's controls are effective
options.B: Advisory: it advises managers on the rival's risks and controls
options.C: A wider role: it needs board-approved safeguards before starting
options.D: Advisory: it negotiates remedies for the rival's control gaps

questions.key_concept: Due diligence is an advisory service: the internal auditor advises on the target's risks and controls, gives no assurance, and management decides on the deal.
questions.pre_read: A decision is about to be made by management. Is the function asked for confidence against criteria, or for input to that decision?
questions.correct_explanation: The CIA Part 1 syllabus lists due diligence among the advisory services an internal audit function performs, and the glossary defines advisory services as advice given without assurance and without management responsibility. Here the function feeds what it sees of the rival's risks and controls into a decision that stays with management. Concluding that those controls are effective, the closest choice, would be assurance, which needs criteria and enough evidence about another company's processes.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a conclusion on effectiveness is assurance. Due diligence input is advice to those deciding on the purchase, and it claims no assurance over the rival.
wrong_explanations.C: Board-approved safeguards belong to a role beyond internal auditing, such as running a function. Advising a deal team is an advisory engagement, an internal audit service.
wrong_explanations.D: Negotiating terms with the rival is the deal team's job. Doing it would be taking on management responsibility, which advisory work never includes.

tips: Eliminate: C, because advising a deal team is an internal audit service and not a wider role, and D, because negotiating with the rival is management's job, not advice.
Final two: B beats A because due diligence input is advice for management's decision; concluding that the rival's controls are effective would be assurance, which this work does not give.
Exam cue: the syllabus lists due diligence under advisory services. So think advice: input on risks and controls, no assurance, and the decision stays with management.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. A request to look ahead
questions.question: A Uruguayan dairy's audit committee asks chief audit executive Lucía how a carbon-pricing law due in three years could affect the business. Which reply BEST fits the Purpose of Internal Auditing?

options.A: Decline: insight and foresight come from audits of running processes
options.B: Decline: weighing the law's effect is management's risk work
options.C: Accept, as an assurance engagement against the law's terms
options.D: Accept: a view on an emerging risk is foresight it can give

questions.key_concept: Internal auditing gives the board and management assurance, advice, insight and foresight. A view on an emerging risk is foresight; management still decides the response.
questions.pre_read: The Purpose Statement names four things internal auditing gives. Are all of them about what already exists?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain I's Purpose Statement says internal auditing gives the board and management assurance, advice, insight and foresight, so a forward-looking view on an emerging risk sits inside its purpose. Giving that view takes on no management responsibility: management still decides how to respond. Calling the law's effect management's risk work, the closest choice, confuses offering a view on a risk with managing it, which does stay with management.

wrong_explanations.A: Insight and foresight can draw on audit work, but the Purpose Statement does not confine them to it. Internal auditing is not limited to what already runs.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: management does own and manage risk. A view on how a future law could affect the business informs management's decisions without taking them over.
wrong_explanations.C: Assurance concludes on an existing condition against criteria. The committee asked how a future law could affect the business, which is a view ahead, not a conclusion on what exists.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the Purpose Statement does not tie insight and foresight to finished audits, and C, because the committee wants a view ahead, not a conclusion on existing processes against criteria.
Final two: D beats B because giving foresight on a risk is internal auditing's own work, while managing that risk, which stays with management, is a different act.
Exam cue: the Purpose Statement names assurance, advice, insight and foresight. A request to look ahead is still internal auditing, as long as management keeps the decision.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. Who answers for conformance
questions.question: Joining a Croatian shipyard's internal audit team, internal auditor Ivana hears that conformance with the Standards is the chief audit executive's concern, not the staff's. Which division of responsibility is MOST accurate?

options.A: Staff for their own work; the chief audit executive for the function
options.B: Every auditor for every standard, function-level ones included
options.C: The chief audit executive for conformance; staff for following methodologies
options.D: The board for conformance, through its oversight of the chief audit executive

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive is accountable for the whole function's conformance; every internal auditor is responsible for the standards that apply to their own work.
questions.pre_read: The Standards bind the function and each person in it. Which parts fall to whom?
questions.correct_explanation: Under the Fundamentals, the chief audit executive answers for the whole function meeting every principle and standard, while each internal auditor answers for the ones that touch their own work, chiefly the ethics and engagement standards. Standard 4.1 adds that every internal auditor must follow both the Standards and the function's methodologies. Leaving staff only the methodologies, the closest choice, drops that personal duty to the Standards.

wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive answers for every standard, including governing and managing the function. Other internal auditors answer for the standards on their own work, mainly Domains II and V.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: following the methodologies is required, but so is following the Standards. Standard 4.1 puts both duties on each internal auditor, not on the chief audit executive alone.
wrong_explanations.D: The board supports and oversees the function, but the Standards bind internal auditors. Accountability for the function's conformance sits with the chief audit executive.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the standards on governing and managing the function fall to the chief audit executive, and D, because the Standards bind internal auditors, not the board.
Final two: A beats C because each internal auditor must follow the Standards as well as the methodologies, while the chief audit executive answers for the function as a whole.
Exam cue: conformance has two levels. The chief audit executive answers for the whole function; each internal auditor answers for the ethics and engagement standards in their own work.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. The public interest in a private company
questions.question: A director of a family-owned Indonesian bus company says the public interest has no bearing on its internal audit function, as it has no outside investors. Which reply by chief audit executive Wayan is BEST?

options.A: It has none: the public interest concerns public-sector bodies
options.B: It does: internal auditors report breaches of law to the authorities directly
options.C: It does: internal auditing helps the company serve the public interest
options.D: It has none: serving the public falls to external auditors and regulators

questions.key_concept: One of the five gains the Purpose Statement lists is the organization's ability to serve the public interest. It holds whoever owns the organization.
questions.pre_read: The Purpose Statement lists five things internal auditing enhances. Does the last one depend on who owns the organization?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain I lists five things internal auditing enhances, and the last is the organization's ability to serve the public interest. The Fundamentals add that its work builds trust in the organization beyond its walls, and the Standards apply in every sector. Limiting the public interest to public-sector bodies, the closest choice, mistakes the Standards' extra public sector guidance for a limit on this benefit.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Standards add guidance for the public sector, but Domain I lists serving the public interest among the gains for every organization, whoever owns it.
wrong_explanations.B: Legal violations go to people or bodies with authority to act, as laws, regulations and policies direct. That is not always an outside authority, nor the benefit at issue.
wrong_explanations.D: External auditors and regulators do serve outside parties, but internal auditing still adds its own part: the Purpose Statement lists serving the public interest among its gains.

tips: Eliminate: B, because legal violations go through the channels that laws, regulations and policies set, and D, because the work of external auditors and regulators does not cancel internal auditing's own contribution.
Final two: C beats A because the Purpose Statement lists serving the public interest among internal auditing's gains in every organization; the public sector section adds guidance, not a limit.
Exam cue: know the five gains in the Purpose Statement: objectives met; governance, risk and control; decisions and oversight; reputation; and the public interest. Ownership changes none of them.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A required clause among recommended ones
questions.question: After managers at a Namibian fishing company kept delaying answers to auditors, chief audit executive Ndapewa drafts four new charter clauses. Which clause do the Standards MOST clearly require?

options.A: How internal auditors obtain the records and people they need
options.B: The chief audit executive's yearly confirmation of independence to the board
options.C: When auditors talk with managers before, during and after engagements
options.D: The board's expectations of management's support for internal audit

questions.key_concept: The charter's mandate must state the board's responsibilities and its expectations of management's support. Access and communication timing are topics to consider.
questions.pre_read: Standard 6.2 sets a minimum for the charter, then lists other topics worth covering. Which list holds each clause?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 requires the charter's mandate to state the board's responsibilities and its expectations of management's support for the internal audit function. How access works and when auditors talk with management are topics the considerations suggest, and the yearly independence confirmation is a separate Standard 7.1 duty. The access clause, the closest choice, fits these delays well, but the Standards list it as a topic to consider, not as minimum content.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: access suits the problem, and the mandate's authority supports it. But how access is obtained is a topic Standard 6.2's considerations suggest, not part of the minimum.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 7.1 does require a yearly confirmation of independence to the board, but as a duty the chief audit executive performs, not as content Standard 6.2 requires in the charter.
wrong_explanations.C: Expectations for communicating with management before, during and after engagements are a recommended charter topic, not content Standard 6.2 requires.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the yearly independence confirmation is a Standard 7.1 duty, not charter content, and C, because the timing of communication with management is a recommended topic, not minimum content.
Final two: D beats A because the mandate must state the board's expectations of management's support, while how access is obtained is a topic the considerations suggest.

Exam cue: the charter's minimum has four parts: the purpose, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate with scope, services and the board's expectations of management, and position and reporting lines.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A new chief audit executive and the charter
questions.question: Rūta becomes chief audit executive of a Lithuanian water utility; its board-approved charter is next due for review under the agreed three-year cycle in 18 months. What is Rūta's BEST step on the charter?

options.A: Keep the charter as approved until the agreed review date
options.B: Review the charter with the board now to consider any changes
options.C: Ask senior management to confirm the charter still fits its expectations
options.D: Leave the review to the board, since it is the board's duty

questions.key_concept: A new chief audit executive is a change that calls for reviewing the charter with the board, whatever the agreed regular cycle.
questions.pre_read: An agreed review cycle is a leading practice. Which events call for a review of the charter outside it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2's essential conditions have the board review the charter with the chief audit executive when things change, and they name the arrival of a new chief audit executive as one example. Standard 6.1 also requires the chief audit executive to assess whether changed circumstances justify discussing the mandate. Waiting for the agreed cycle, the closest choice, follows a leading practice and passes over the trigger the Standards name.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: an agreed cycle is a leading practice. The Standards also call for review when things change, and they name a new chief audit executive as such a change.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management's expectations feed into the charter, but the review the Standards name is held with the board, which alone approves any change.
wrong_explanations.D: Board duties are essential conditions, so the chief audit executive raises them rather than waits. Standard 6.1 also requires the chief audit executive to assess changes and seek discussion.

tips: Eliminate: C, because senior management gives input while the review is held by the board, and D, because the chief audit executive raises the board's duties instead of waiting for them.
Final two: B beats A because a new chief audit executive is a change the Standards name as a reason to review the charter, whatever the agreed cycle says.
Exam cue: a regular review cycle is a floor, not a ceiling. A new chief audit executive, new risks or a major reorganization bring the charter back to the board early.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A new administrative line and the charter
questions.question: The chief executive of a Canadian grain cooperative tells chief audit executive Émile to report administratively to the finance director from next month and to update the charter. What is Émile's BEST response?

options.A: Refer the change to the board, which sets the charter's reporting lines
options.B: Update the charter, as administrative matters run through management
options.C: Decline, as the administrative line must run to the chief executive
options.D: Accept, and propose safeguards for audits of finance areas

questions.key_concept: The charter records the reporting relationships the board determines. A change to the administrative line goes to the board, not just into a charter edit.
questions.pre_read: Who determines the reporting relationships written into the charter, and who approves changes to the charter?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 requires the chief audit executive to document in the charter the reporting relationships the board has determined, and Standard 6.2 makes the board the approver of the charter and its changes. So a new administrative line is the board's call. Treating it as a management matter, the closest choice, mixes up routine administration, which runs through management, with the reporting line itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: expenses, leave and similar administration do run through the administrative line. Which line that is, and the charter that records it, are for the board to decide.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting administratively to the chief executive is a leading practice, not a requirement. Another senior officer can work with safeguards, if the board so decides.
wrong_explanations.D: Safeguards would be needed, as internal audit covers finance areas, but accepting first bypasses the board, which determines the reporting lines and approves the charter change.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a chief executive line is a leading practice, not a must, and D, because safeguards follow the board's decision on the line and do not replace it.
Final two: A beats B because the board determines the reporting relationships the charter records; management handles routine administration within the line the board has set.
Exam cue: the board decides where internal audit sits and approves every charter change. Management may propose a new line; it cannot put one in place.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. An exclusion asked for in advisory work
questions.question: A Cambodian hotel group's finance head asks internal auditor Sokha for advisory work on a draft travel-booking process, leaving out mileage claims, which a new system will replace. How should Sokha BEST treat the exclusion?

options.A: As a scope limitation to discuss with the finance head, then elevate
options.B: As a conflicting demand for the chief audit executive to report
options.C: As a scope limitation to explain in the final communication
options.D: As agreed scope, settled with the finance head who requested it

questions.key_concept: Advisory work's nature and scope are agreed with the requester, so a requested exclusion is agreed scope. Scope limitations are conditions of assurance engagements.
questions.pre_read: Standard 13.3 defines scope limitations for one kind of engagement. Which kind, and how is advisory scope set?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary and the Domain V introduction make the nature and scope of advisory services a matter of agreement with the party requesting them, and Standard 13.3's considerations say advisory objectives and scope are typically set jointly. Standard 13.3 defines scope limitations as conditions of assurance engagements. So the exclusion is agreed scope, which the chief audit executive still approves, not a limitation to discuss and elevate, the closest choice.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: auditors should weigh whether a requested exclusion is a scope limitation, but Standard 13.3 defines those as assurance conditions. In advisory work, requester and auditors agree the scope.
wrong_explanations.B: A conflicting demand arises when requests clash with planned services, such as swapping planned assurance for advice. Leaving one step out of requested advice is not one.
wrong_explanations.C: Final communications explain scope limitations for assurance engagements. Advisory work states its agreed objectives and scope, and this exclusion is part of them.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a conflicting demand clashes with planned services, and C, because explaining scope limitations belongs to the final communication of assurance engagements.
Final two: D beats A because scope limitations are assurance conditions; in advisory work the requester and the internal auditors agree what the work covers.

Exam cue: check the engagement type before calling anything a scope limitation. In assurance, a restriction is discussed and, if unresolved, elevated; in advisory work, scope is agreed with whoever asked.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. Assurance asked for where no criteria exist
questions.question: The board of a Moldovan winery wants assurance that its new remote-work policy is working, but management never set any measures of the policy's success. What should internal auditor Elena do FIRST?

options.A: Propose advisory work to help management set measures of success
options.B: Adopt the measures that peer wineries use for remote-work policies
options.C: Agree suitable criteria with senior management, the board or both
options.D: Report the missing measures to the board as an engagement finding

questions.key_concept: With no adequate criteria from management, internal auditors must settle suitable ones by discussing them with the board, senior management or both. Advice may follow.
questions.pre_read: Assurance compares a condition with criteria. With whom must criteria be settled when management has set none?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 13.4, internal auditors must first judge whether the board and senior management have set adequate criteria; where they have not, the auditors must agree suitable ones in talks with the board, senior management or both. Its considerations add that those talks may end in a choice of advisory work instead. Proposing advice, the closest choice, is a possible outcome of the required discussion, not a step ahead of it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Standards say a discussion about missing criteria may lead to advisory work. That is a possible outcome of the required discussion, not a step ahead of it.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer practice can inform criteria, but Standard 13.4 has internal auditors settle criteria by discussing them with the board, senior management or both, not adopt them alone.
wrong_explanations.D: A finding is a gap between criteria and condition. With no criteria yet, there is nothing to measure the policy against, so a finding cannot come first.

tips: Eliminate: B, because criteria are settled by discussing them with the board, senior management or both, not borrowed alone, and D, because a finding needs criteria to measure the condition against.
Final two: C beats A because the discussion of criteria is required, while a switch to advisory work is only a possible result of that discussion.
Exam cue: no criteria, no assurance. First settle criteria with senior management, the board or both; then decide whether assurance can go ahead or advice fits better.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A Topical Requirement met during another engagement
questions.question: In an assurance engagement on a Tunisian olive exporter's payroll, internal auditor Amira finds shared administrator passwords, a control failure that creates significant cybersecurity risk. How does the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement apply MOST accurately?

options.A: Every requirement applies, since the topic arose in assurance work
options.B: Those that fit the risk apply, and each exclusion's reason is documented
options.C: As recommended practice, since payroll is the engagement's subject
options.D: Not yet: it applies when a cybersecurity engagement enters the plan

questions.key_concept: A Topical Requirement applies when its topic surfaces in assurance work. Every requirement is assessed, and the rationale for each exclusion is documented.
questions.pre_read: A Topical Requirement can apply when its topic was never planned. Must every requirement in it then be applied?
questions.correct_explanation: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement applies when its topic is identified while performing an engagement, and it is mandatory for assurance services. It also says not every requirement may apply in an engagement: each is assessed for applicability, and a rationale is documented for any excluded. The application guidance adds that a risk confined to controls may call only for the control requirements. Applying every requirement, the closest choice, overlooks that.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: conformance is mandatory for assurance, yet not every requirement must be applied. Each is assessed, and those that do not fit the risk are excluded with documented reasons.
wrong_explanations.C: Conformance is recommended for advisory services. This is an assurance engagement, and identifying the topic during it is one of the three cases in which the requirement applies.
wrong_explanations.D: A planned engagement on the topic is one trigger, not the sole one. Identifying the topic while performing an engagement is another.

tips: Eliminate: C, because recommended conformance is for advisory work, and D, because identifying the topic during an engagement already triggers the requirement.
Final two: B beats A because each requirement is assessed for applicability, and those that do not fit the risk are excluded with the reason documented.
Exam cue: a Topical Requirement is triggered three ways: planned, found during an engagement, or requested. Mandatory for assurance means every requirement is assessed, not that every one is applied.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Process mapping inside an assurance engagement
questions.question: Planning an assurance engagement on a Zambian sugar estate's fuel issuing, internal auditor Mwila decides to map the process from tank delivery to vehicle. How should this mapping BEST be treated?

options.A: As advisory work, with its scope agreed with the fuel manager
options.B: As a second-line task that needs safeguards before internal audit does it
options.C: As a separate engagement whose scope the chief audit executive approves
options.D: As part of understanding the activity before testing begins

questions.key_concept: Mapping a process to understand it is part of assurance planning. The same mapping is advisory work when it is delivered to management as advice.
questions.pre_read: The same tool can serve two purposes. Is this map the service, or a way to understand the activity?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 requires internal auditors to understand the activity under review, including how its processes are meant to work, before assessing its risks; its considerations mention charts, process narratives and walk-throughs as tools. Here the map serves Mwila's own assurance planning. Process mapping is an advisory service, the closest choice, when the map is delivered to management as advice, whoever proposed it, which is not the purpose here.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: mapping is an advisory service when the map is delivered to management as advice. Here it is a planning tool inside assurance work, whose scope auditors mainly set.
wrong_explanations.B: Second-line roles support, monitor and challenge management's handling of risk. Drawing a map to understand a process takes on no management responsibility, so no such safeguards arise.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive approves each engagement's objectives and scope. Mapping for planning is a step within this engagement, not a separate one with its own approval.

tips: Eliminate: B, because mapping to understand a process takes on no management responsibility, and C, because the mapping is a step within this engagement, not a new engagement.
Final two: D beats A because understanding the activity is a required planning step of assurance work; mapping is an advisory service when the map itself is the advice management receives.
Exam cue: name the purpose, not the tool. A map drawn to understand or test an activity is part of assurance; the same map delivered as help to management is advisory work.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Giving training or owning a training program
questions.question: An Icelandic insurer's chief executive asks chief audit executive Sigrún to take over, permanently, the compliance team's mandatory training program: setting its content, enrolling staff and certifying completion to the regulator. Which description fits BEST?

options.A: A role beyond internal auditing, with its safeguards in the charter
options.B: An advisory service, as training is one the Standards name
options.C: A temporary role, with outside assurance until 12 months after it ends
options.D: An assurance service, as the regulator relies on its completion records

questions.key_concept: Giving training is advisory work. Owning a training program, down to certifying it to a regulator, is a role beyond internal auditing.
questions.pre_read: Advisory services give advice without taking on management responsibility. Does running this program stay on the advice side of that line?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary lists training as an advisory service, given without taking on management responsibility. Sigrún would instead own a compliance program, from content to certifying completion to the regulator: a role beyond internal auditing. Standard 7.1 requires discussing it with the board and senior management and, as it is ongoing, recording it and its safeguards in the board-approved charter. Calling it advisory, the closest choice, misses the ownership.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: training is an advisory service when internal auditors give it as advice. Owning the program and certifying it to a regulator takes on management's responsibility.
wrong_explanations.C: Outside assurance until 12 months after the role ends is the safeguard for a temporary role. This one is permanent, so its safeguards belong in the charter.
wrong_explanations.D: An assurance service is an objective assessment against criteria. Here Sigrún would run the program and certify it, not assess it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because outside assurance for 12 months after the role is the safeguard for temporary roles, and D, because running and certifying a program is not assessing it.
Final two: A beats B because training given as advice is advisory, but owning the program and certifying it takes on management responsibility, which makes it a role beyond internal auditing.
Exam cue: ask who owns the outcome. If internal audit advises and management decides, it is advisory work; if internal audit would own and run it, it is a role beyond internal auditing.
