questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A governing structure that limits independence
questions.question: A Paraguayan farm cooperative's members elect a board of its department heads, whose areas internal audit reviews; chief audit executive Sofía reports to that board. What is MOST clearly required of Sofía?

options.A: Record the reasons a condition is agreed unnecessary, and its substitute
options.B: Document how the structure limits independence, and possible safeguards
options.C: Tell the board that the function cannot conform with the Standards
options.D: Arrange independent outside assurance over the areas board members manage

questions.key_concept: When the governing structure itself does not support independence, the chief audit executive must document what limits it and the safeguards that could be used.
questions.pre_read: Several documenting duties exist for gaps in governance. Which one fits a structure that cannot support independence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 sets a duty for this case: when the governing structure cannot support the function's independence, the chief audit executive must record what in it limits independence and which safeguards could help. A board of the managers whose areas internal audit reviews is such a structure. Concluding the function cannot conform, the closest choice, is a step the Domain III introduction allows, not requires, when the reasons for an unmet essential condition are disputed.

wrong_explanations.A: That record is required when the chief audit executive, the board and senior management agree an essential condition is unnecessary. No such agreement is described here.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Domain III allows, not requires, that conclusion when the reasons for an unmet essential condition are disputed. Standard 7.1's documented limits and safeguards answer this structure.
wrong_explanations.D: Alternative assurance is required over areas internal audit would review that the chief audit executive runs beyond internal auditing. Here the issue is the board's makeup.

tips: Eliminate: A, because that record follows an agreement that an essential condition is unnecessary, and D, because alternative assurance is for areas the chief audit executive is responsible for beyond internal auditing.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 7.1 requires documenting the structure's limits and possible safeguards, while concluding nonconformance is an option tied to disputed essential conditions.

Exam cue: match each documenting duty to its trigger. A structure limiting independence: its limits and safeguards (must). An agreed unneeded condition: reasons and substitutes (must). A disputed one: why it is refused (should).

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. Contracted auditors and the Standards
questions.question: A Bolivian miner cosources its IT engagements; the outside firm's lead tells internal auditor Rosa its staff follow the firm's own method, not the Standards. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: They bind the firm's staff once the firm's contract adopts them
options.B: They bind the firm's staff in assurance work, not in advice
options.C: They bind the firm's staff for the internal audit work they do
options.D: They bind the chief audit executive in place of the firm's staff

questions.key_concept: The Standards bind anyone who provides internal audit services, whether employed in-house or contracted through an outside provider.
questions.pre_read: Do the Standards cover only an organization's own employees, or everyone who provides its internal audit services?
questions.correct_explanation: The fundamentals of the Standards extend them to anyone doing internal audit work for an organization: its own staff, auditors hired through an outside firm, or both together. The firm's staff are doing that work here, so the Standards bind them. The closest choice is half right: the chief audit executive answers for the whole function's conformance, but that does not release the people who do the work.

wrong_explanations.A: The Standards apply because the work is internal auditing, not because a contract names them. A contract can add duties for a provider; it cannot switch the Standards off.
wrong_explanations.B: That split belongs to Topical Requirements, which assurance work must follow and advisory work is advised to follow. The Standards themselves cover both kinds of service, unless one says otherwise.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the chief audit executive answers for the function's conformance, contracted work included. That sits on top of each provider's own duty to conform; it does not replace it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the Standards follow the work whatever a contract says, and B, because the assurance-only split belongs to Topical Requirements, not to the Standards themselves.
Final two: C beats D because the chief audit executive's accountability for the function sits on top of each provider's own duty to conform; it does not replace that duty.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, who is bound follows what work is done. Anyone providing internal audit services, employed or contracted, conforms with the Standards.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Purpose of Internal Auditing. A small function and the Standards
questions.question: Ani, chief audit executive of an Armenian brandy distiller, says that because the internal audit function has only two people, it may treat the Standards as optional guidance. Which reply is BEST?

options.A: Conformance is expected; an unmet requirement needs explained alternatives
options.B: A requirement becomes optional once the board agrees that it is unnecessary
options.C: Conformance is expected with Domains II and V; III and IV guide
options.D: Conformance is expected, so any work the team cannot do is outsourced

questions.key_concept: Conformance is expected whatever the function's size. For a requirement that truly cannot be met, the chief audit executive documents and explains alternatives and impact.
questions.pre_read: Size can make some requirements hard to meet. Does that make the Standards optional, and what happens to a requirement that cannot be met?
questions.correct_explanation: The fundamentals expect conformance from every function and accept that small ones may find some tasks hard. When a requirement truly cannot be met, alternative actions should aim at its intent, and Standard 4.1 requires the chief audit executive to document and communicate the circumstance, the alternatives, their impact and the rationale. The closest choice describes essential conditions, which the board and senior management may agree are unnecessary; requirements are never set aside that way.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an agreement that something is unnecessary, with documented reasons and substitutes, is the route for essential conditions placed on the board and senior management, not for requirements.
wrong_explanations.C: Domains II and V hold most of each internal auditor's duties, but Domains III and IV contain requirements too, and the chief audit executive answers for every domain.
wrong_explanations.D: Outsourcing is one way to obtain missing skills. It is not the Standards' answer to every requirement a small function cannot meet.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the chief audit executive answers for conformance with every domain, and D, because outsourcing obtains missing skills and is not the route for each unmet requirement.
Final two: A beats B because an unmet requirement has one route, documented and communicated alternatives; agreeing that something is unnecessary applies only to essential conditions.
Exam cue: an unmet requirement is documented and explained, never declared optional; an unneeded essential condition is agreed and documented. Match the route to what is missing.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. How often the mandate is discussed
questions.question: Kofi, a Togolese brewery's chief audit executive, checks yearly whether changes call for a mandate discussion, and this year's check found none; a board member says one is required yearly. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: A discussion is required every year, whatever has changed
options.B: A discussion is required once The IIA notably revises the Standards
options.C: A discussion is required once the board's membership changes
options.D: A discussion is required once changed circumstances justify one

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must periodically assess whether changes justify discussing the mandate, and discuss it when they do; a yearly look is preferred practice.
questions.pre_read: Which part of keeping the mandate current is the requirement: the periodic check, or a discussion with the board every year?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.1's requirement has two parts: a periodic check on whether changed circumstances call for a mandate discussion with the board and senior management, and that discussion when the check says yes. The considerations add a should: weigh such changes formally at least yearly, which Kofi does. The closest choice turns the yearly check into a yearly discussion; the Standards tie the discussion to change, not to the calendar.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the yearly element is the chief audit executive's check, a preferred practice. The discussion itself is required when that check finds changes that justify one.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 6.1's considerations say a notable revision of the Standards may justify a mandate discussion. The must is the periodic check, and a discussion only when it finds one justified.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 6.1's considerations list significant board changes among things that may justify a discussion; the periodic check weighs them. A change of members triggers nothing automatically.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because a revision of the Standards or a board change may justify a discussion, which the periodic check weighs; neither requires one automatically.
Final two: D beats A because the requirement is the periodic check plus a discussion when changes justify one; the yearly look is preferred practice, and the discussion follows changes.
Exam cue: separate a check from the action it may lead to. A required periodic assessment is met even when, nothing having changed, no action follows.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A second set of standards and the charter
questions.question: A national law requires the internal auditors of a Kazakh state railway to follow a national public-sector audit standard. How should chief audit executive Aigerim BEST reflect this in the charter?

options.A: Commit to the national standard in place of the Global Standards
options.B: Keep the commitment to the Global Standards, and name the national one
options.C: Commit to whichever of the two sets is stricter on each point
options.D: Name the national standard, and cite the Global Standards in the methodologies

questions.key_concept: The charter must commit the function to the Global Internal Audit Standards. Another set that law adds sits beside that commitment, never in its place.
questions.pre_read: Every charter carries a required commitment to the Standards. What happens to it when a law adds a second set of audit standards?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 makes the commitment to adhere to the Global Internal Audit Standards part of every charter's minimum content, so another set cannot replace it. Where law shapes the work, the charter may explain how both the law and the Standards are met, and Standard 4.1 has communications cite other requirements used alongside. Following the stricter rule where the two differ, the closest choice, is allowed; it does not remove the required commitment.

wrong_explanations.A: The commitment to the Global Internal Audit Standards is required charter content. A law can add a second set of standards; it does not take that commitment away.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: where two sets differ, a function may follow the stricter rule. The charter must still state its commitment to the Global Internal Audit Standards by name.
wrong_explanations.D: Methodologies must align with the Standards, but the commitment to the Global Internal Audit Standards is required charter content; moving it to the methodologies leaves the charter short.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a second set adds to the required commitment and cannot replace it, and D, because the commitment to the Global Standards belongs in the charter itself, not the methodologies.
Final two: B beats C because the charter must name the commitment to the Global Internal Audit Standards; following the stricter rule point by point is practice, not a substitute for it.
Exam cue: required charter content is a floor. Laws, other standards or board wishes can be added to it; none of them takes a required item out.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. Widening an assurance engagement's scope
questions.question: Midway through assurance work on a Tanzanian safari firm's vehicle-parts buying, internal auditor Neema finds a third bought on staff cards, outside scope; the parts manager objects to widening it. What is Neema's BEST course?

options.A: Widen the scope with the chief audit executive's approval; tell the manager
options.B: Widen the scope if the parts manager agrees to the change
options.C: Keep the scope; the chief audit executive elevates the objection
options.D: Keep the scope, and propose the card purchases for next year's plan

questions.key_concept: In assurance work, internal auditors may change the scope as the work requires; the chief audit executive approves the change, and management is told promptly.
questions.pre_read: Once assurance work is under way, who decides whether its scope changes: internal audit, with its own approval, or the manager under review?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 lets internal auditors change an engagement's objectives and scope when the work shows a need, requires the scope to be enough to meet the objectives, and requires the chief audit executive to approve each change; Standard 13.1 requires telling management of changes in time. A third of parts spend sits inside parts buying. The closest choice, the manager's agreement, is how advisory scope is set, not assurance scope.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: advisory work's nature and scope are agreed with the party that requested it. In assurance, internal auditors set and change the scope, with the chief audit executive's approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Requests to exclude items should be weighed as possible scope limitations, but the chief audit executive elevates one only if it blocks work and discussion fails. This objection does neither.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring suits a matter outside what this engagement must cover. A third of parts spend is part of parts buying, so the scope would fall short of the objective.

tips: Eliminate: C, because an objection that blocks no work is discussed, not elevated as a scope limitation, and D, because a third of parts spend belongs inside an engagement on parts buying.
Final two: A beats B because in assurance work internal auditors set and change the scope with the chief audit executive's approval; agreement with the manager is how advisory scope is set.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, assurance scope belongs to internal audit, approved by the chief audit executive and communicated to management; advisory scope is agreed with whoever asked for the work.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A regulator's objective inside an operational audit
questions.question: A regulator requires a Jamaican pension fund's internal auditors to report yearly on crediting contributions within five days; this year's only contributions engagement is a cost audit. How should internal auditor Kemar BEST treat this?

options.A: Weigh it in the engagement risk assessment beside the cost risks
options.B: Leave it to compliance, which monitors the fund's regulatory rules
options.C: Include it among the engagement's objectives, beside the cost ones
options.D: Agree with the contributions manager whether the engagement covers it

questions.key_concept: Engagement objectives must include goals that laws or regulations mandate, so one engagement can join a regulator's compliance objective to operational ones.
questions.pre_read: Engagement objectives usually follow the engagement risk assessment. Is any objective included whatever that assessment ranks?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 requires engagement objectives to state the engagement's purpose and specific goals, including those that laws or regulations mandate. With the regulator's report due and no other contributions engagement this year, Kemar builds it into the objectives, so the engagement becomes part operational audit and part regulatory compliance audit. Weighing it in the risk assessment, the closest choice, is how most objectives are chosen, but a mandated goal goes in whatever the ranking says.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the engagement risk assessment shapes most objectives. A goal that a law or regulation mandates is an objective whatever the ranking shows.
wrong_explanations.B: Compliance monitoring is a second-line role for management. The regulator asked for internal audit's report, which that monitoring cannot replace.
wrong_explanations.D: Agreeing coverage with the requesting manager fits advisory work. Assurance objectives are set by internal auditors and approved by the chief audit executive.

tips: Eliminate: B, because second-line monitoring cannot replace the report the regulator requires from internal audit, and D, because assurance objectives are not agreed with the manager under review.
Final two: C beats A because objectives must include goals that laws or regulations mandate; the risk assessment ranks everything else but cannot rank a mandated goal out.
Exam cue: when a law or regulator names what internal audit must cover, treat it as a fixed objective. Risk-based judgment shapes the rest of the engagement around it.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Presenting a benchmarking gap
questions.question: As advisory work for a Romanian bakery group's operations chief, internal auditor Ioana finds its cost per invoice 40% above five peers', though within management's budget. How should Ioana BEST present the gap?

options.A: As a finding, with the peers' average cost as the criterion
options.B: As a comparison, with the differences for management to weigh
options.C: As a risk accepted above tolerance, to raise with senior management
options.D: As a comparison, with the peers' practices as the team's new standard

questions.key_concept: Benchmarking in advisory work compares; it does not set the rule. Internal auditors explain the differences, and management decides whether the peers' practices fit.
questions.pre_read: A gap against peers looks like a shortfall. Is a peer figure a criterion, a target, or a comparison for management to weigh?
questions.correct_explanation: The Part 1 syllabus lists benchmarking among advisory services, which give advice without assurance or management responsibility: Ioana explains the differences, and management decides. A finding needs a gap from evaluation criteria, and under Standard 13.4 the criteria start from those the board and senior management have set; here management's own budget was met. Treating the peers' average as the criterion, the closest choice, imposes a yardstick nobody adopted.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: industry benchmarks can be criteria, but management's adequate measures come first, and others are set through discussion with senior management or the board. Here the budget was met.
wrong_explanations.C: Escalation applies when management accepts risk above the organization's appetite or tolerance. A cost within management's own budget shows no such acceptance.
wrong_explanations.D: Making peers' practices the team's standard is a management decision, and differences in size, risk and strategy may make them a poor fit.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a cost within management's own budget is not risk accepted beyond tolerance, and D, because adopting peers' practices as the standard is management's decision, not the adviser's.
Final two: B beats A because a finding measures a gap from agreed criteria; here the only agreed measure, the budget, was met, so the peer gap is information to weigh.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a benchmark is a comparison until someone with authority adopts it as a criterion or target. The internal auditor explains it; management decides.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. The departing chief audit executive and the successor's qualifications
questions.question: Nino, chief audit executive of a Georgian wine exporter, retires next year, and its audit committee is starting the search for a successor. What is MOST clearly required of Nino?

options.A: Sharing a succession plan for the role with the committee
options.B: Approving the job description the committee drafts for the role
options.C: Joining the interviews and ranking the shortlisted candidates
options.D: Explaining, with examples, which qualifications the role needs

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive must explain to the board what qualifications and competencies the role needs; the board approves the role and names the qualifications.
questions.pre_read: Several people take part in replacing a chief audit executive. Sort what the Standards require of the current one from what they only recommend.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.2 requires the chief audit executive to explain to the board, with examples, which qualifications and skills a chief audit executive needs, so Nino must do that. The board approves the role and names the qualifications, and authorizes the appointment with senior management's input. Sharing a succession plan, the closest choice, is a should in the considerations of Standards 7.2 and 10.2; it is not the requirement.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: sharing a succession plan with the board is a should in the considerations of Standards 7.2 and 10.2. Nino's requirement is explaining the qualifications the role needs.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 7.2's considerations let the board itself look over and sign off the job description. That sign-off is the board's step, not the departing chief audit executive's.
wrong_explanations.C: Board members are encouraged to take part in interviews, and the board authorizes the appointment with senior management's input. Selecting is not Nino's to do.

tips: Eliminate: B, because approving the job description is the board's step, and C, because interviewing and ranking candidates belong to the board and senior management, not the departing chief audit executive.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 7.2 requires explaining the qualifications the role needs; sharing a succession plan with the board is a should, not the requirement.
Exam cue: when the board decides something about internal audit, look for the chief audit executive's duty to inform that decision. Informing is required; deciding stays with the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. After a session without senior management
questions.question: After a private session with a Malawian tea estate's audit committee on staffing gaps and next year's coverage, the chief executive asks chief audit executive Chikondi what was discussed. What is Chikondi's BEST response?

options.A: Decline, as sessions without senior management are kept from it
options.B: Decline, and note the request in the yearly independence confirmation
options.C: Brief the chief executive, whose approval the coverage changes need
options.D: Brief the chief executive on the resourcing and coverage points

questions.key_concept: A private board session protects a channel, not a secret: senior management should hear what was discussed, unless it concerns, say, a senior manager's misconduct.
questions.pre_read: Private sessions protect the chief audit executive's access to the board. Does that make everything said there secret from senior management?
questions.correct_explanation: Private sessions give the chief audit executive a channel to the board, not a duty of secrecy. Standard 9.4 requires the plan and the effect of resource limits on coverage to be shared with senior management, and Standard 6.3 requires board communications to be coordinated with it; its considerations add that private talks are passed on unless the subject is, say, a senior manager's misconduct. Declining, the closest choice, fits only that case.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: withholding fits a private session about a senior manager's own conduct. Staffing gaps and coverage are matters Standard 9.4 requires sharing with senior management anyway.
wrong_explanations.B: The yearly confirmation reports incidents that may have impaired independence. A chief executive asking about routine matters is not interference.
wrong_explanations.C: The board approves the internal audit plan and significant changes to it. Senior management gives input on coverage; it does not approve it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a question about routine matters is not an incident that impairs independence, and C, because the board approves coverage changes, with senior management giving input.

Final two: D beats A because private sessions keep the board channel open without a duty of secrecy; withholding fits only a subject like a senior manager's misconduct, and coverage must be shared anyway.
Exam cue: private sessions keep a channel to the board open; they do not shut senior management out. Ask what the session was about before deciding who may hear of it.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A reporting line to the board on paper only
questions.question: A Qatari shipper's charter has chief audit executive Hamad report to the audit committee, but the chief executive edits and presents Hamad's reports at meetings Hamad never attends. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Impaired independence: management stands between Hamad and the board
options.B: No impairment: reporting through the chief executive is leading practice
options.C: Impaired objectivity: Hamad must disclose it to the board
options.D: A scope limitation: Hamad discusses it, then elevates it to the board

questions.key_concept: A functional line to the board that exists only on paper does not support independence. The chief audit executive needs direct communication with the board.
questions.pre_read: A reporting line can be written into the charter and still not work. What makes a functional line to the board real?
questions.correct_explanation: Principle 7 and Standard 7.1 rest independence on the chief audit executive reporting directly to the board, and the considerations list a chief audit executive without direct communication or interaction with the board as a situation that may impair it. Here the chief executive filters and presents Hamad's reports, so the charter's line does not work. Calling it leading practice, the closest choice, confuses it with the administrative line, which the chief executive may hold.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an administrative line to the chief executive is leading practice. The functional line must still run directly to the board, and here it does not.
wrong_explanations.C: Objectivity is each auditor's unbiased mindset. The problem here is the function's position, a matter of independence, not Hamad's personal judgment.
wrong_explanations.D: A scope limitation is a condition inside an engagement, such as restricted access to records. This is a defect in the function's reporting line.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the problem lies in the function's position, not in Hamad's own mindset, and D, because scope limitations are conditions inside an engagement, not a reporting-line defect.
Final two: A beats B because the chief executive may hold the administrative line, but the functional line must reach the board directly, without management editing what the board receives.

Exam cue: judge the line by what happens, not by the charter. If management edits internal audit's reports or stands between the chief audit executive and the board, the functional line is not working.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Where a support department sits
questions.question: At an Omani hospital group, internal auditor Salim must place the HR department, which reports to the chief operating officer and runs hiring and payroll. Under current IIA Three Lines guidance, which placement is BEST?

options.A: Second line: it serves every hospital in the group as shared support
options.B: First line: it reports to a member of senior management
options.C: First line: back-office work is part of running the organization
options.D: Second line: it is organizationally separate from the wards

questions.key_concept: Three Lines: work that runs the organization, back office included, is first line; the second line gives specialist support and challenge on risk.
questions.pre_read: Support departments serve the whole organization. Does that make them second line, or part of running the business?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model counts all work that runs the organization as first line, in back offices as much as on the front line, and keeps the second line for specialist roles that support and challenge on risk. Its notes say some organizations call support departments second line; the model does not. HR's hiring and payroll run operations. Serving every hospital, the closest choice, does not change that.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some organizations do call support departments second line. The 2026 statement puts back-office work in the first line and keeps the second for specialist roles on risk.
wrong_explanations.B: First line is right, but not for that reason. Second-line roles also report to members of senior management, so the reporting line does not decide the placement.
wrong_explanations.D: Separation from operations is a strength of second-line roles, but it does not make a department one. HR's own work is running processes, which is first line.

tips: Eliminate: B, because second-line roles also report to senior managers, so that reason cannot place HR, and D, because separation from the wards does not turn operational work into second-line work.
Final two: C beats A because the 2026 statement places back-office work in the first line; serving many units does not make a department a risk-focused specialist.
Exam cue: place a role by what it does. Running a process is first line; specialist support, monitoring and challenge on risk is second line; independent assurance is third.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Who answers to the board for risk management
questions.question: A Finnish utility's board asks internal auditor Aino who should answer to it for how well risk management, compliance and controls work. Under current IIA Three Lines guidance, who is MOST accountable?

options.A: The chief risk officer, who maintains the risk management framework
options.B: Senior management, which delegates much of the work to others
options.C: The chief audit executive, who gives assurance on those processes
options.D: The board's risk committee, which oversees the risk profile

questions.key_concept: Risk work may go to a second-line chief risk officer; senior management, headed by the chief executive, still answers to the board for it.
questions.pre_read: Many roles touch risk management: a risk function, internal audit and the board. Which one answers to the board for whether it works?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model places accountability to the board for how well risk management, compliance and control work with the senior management team, with the chief executive officer at its head. Management may hand the design and running of those processes to others, such as a chief risk officer in a second-line role, but not its accountability. Internal audit assures; the board oversees.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a chief risk officer may maintain the framework and monitor risks in a second-line role. Accountability to the board for whether processes work stays with senior management.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief audit executive gives the board independent assurance on these processes. Answering for them would put internal audit in management's seat.
wrong_explanations.D: The board and its committees oversee risk management and hold management to account. Accountability runs from management to the board, not within it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because internal audit assures the processes and does not answer for running them, and D, because the board's committees are the overseers to whom management answers.
Final two: B beats A because a chief risk officer runs risk work in a second-line role for management, while senior management, headed by the chief executive officer, stays accountable to the board.
Exam cue: separate who runs a task from who answers for it. Management may delegate risk work to the second line; it cannot delegate its accountability to the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. Oversight once internal audit is outsourced
questions.question: A Montenegrin charity outsources internal audit to a firm whose partner, Milica, acts as chief audit executive; a trustee wants the audit committee to leave oversight to the firm. Which reply by Milica is BEST?

options.A: Yes: the chief audit executive answers for the function's conformance
options.B: No: the audit committee also approves each engagement's scope
options.C: Yes: the firm's own quality reviews already oversee its work
options.D: No: the audit committee's oversight continues under the contract

questions.key_concept: Outsourcing moves the work, not the board's role: the board still supports and oversees the function, while the chief audit executive answers for conformance.
questions.pre_read: The Standards apply whether internal auditors are employees or a contracted firm. What changes for the board when the whole function is outsourced?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III says the Standards apply whether internal auditors are employed, contracted or both, and that in every case backing and overseeing the function remains the board's role. The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement adds that outsourcing leaves the board's accountability unchanged. Milica's own duty for conformance, the closest choice, is real, but it sits beside the board's oversight and does not replace it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a chief audit executive supplied by a firm still answers for conformance. That duty sits beside the board's oversight of the function; it does not take its place.
wrong_explanations.B: The chief audit executive approves each engagement's objectives and scope. The board approves the charter, plan, budget and resource plan, not engagement scopes.
wrong_explanations.C: The firm's quality reviews support conformance, which the chief audit executive answers for. Oversight of the function is the board's, whoever supplies the staff.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the chief audit executive, not the board, approves engagement scopes, and C, because the firm's quality reviews support conformance but never replace the board's oversight.
Final two: D beats A because the chief audit executive's duty for conformance is real but sits beside the board's duty to support and oversee the function, which outsourcing leaves in place.
Exam cue: a contract can change who does internal audit work and who reviews its quality, but the board's oversight of the function stays exactly where it was.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. Which of two governing bodies is the board
questions.question: A Costa Rican state port's ministry council appoints its directors; its founding law gives the directors alone approval of internal audit's charter. Which body should chief audit executive Valeria BEST treat as the board?

options.A: The directors, as the body able to give internal audit its mandate
options.B: The ministry council, as it appoints the directors who approve the charter
options.C: Both bodies jointly, as each acts as a board over the port
options.D: The executive committee, as the group that runs the port each day

questions.key_concept: Where more than one body governs, the board for internal audit is the body authorized to give it its authority, role and responsibilities.
questions.pre_read: The glossary starts from the highest body charged with governance. What decides which body counts when an organization has two?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary deals with organizations that have more than one governing body: for internal audit, the board is whichever body is empowered to give the function its authority, role and responsibilities. The founding law gives charter approval, and with it the mandate, to the directors alone, so they are Valeria's board. The ministry council, the closest choice, appoints the directors, but that does not make it the body that authorizes internal audit.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: appointing the directors gives the council power over them, but with several governing bodies the board is the one empowered to give internal audit its mandate: the directors.
wrong_explanations.C: Two bodies share the board's role only if both are empowered over internal audit. Here the law gives charter approval to the directors alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Reading the board as the people who run the organization fits only where no governing body exists. This port has one empowered over internal audit.

tips: Eliminate: C, because only an empowered body counts and the law empowers the directors alone, and D, because management stands in for the board only where no governing body exists.
Final two: A beats B because, with two governing bodies, the board is the one empowered to give internal audit its mandate; appointing the directors does not make the council that body.

Exam cue: when an organization has layers of governing bodies, ask which one is empowered to give internal audit its authority, role and responsibilities, usually by approving the charter. That body is the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. A refused essential condition the chief audit executive cannot accept
questions.question: A Swiss watchmaker's audit committee refuses yearly talks on whether internal audit's resources suffice; chief audit executive Luca showed examples of the harm, offered alternatives and rejects its reasons. What is Luca's BEST next step?

options.A: Show the committee, with examples, how the missing talks will hurt
options.B: Record the committee's reasons and the conditions that compensate
options.C: Document the committee's reasons and share them, assessor included
options.D: Accept the refusal, as the Standards place no requirement on boards

questions.key_concept: If the chief audit executive rejects why the board refuses an essential condition, the reasons should be recorded, shared and kept for the external assessor.
questions.pre_read: Domain III sets out what happens when the board will not provide an essential condition. Which step fits once examples and alternatives have failed?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III's introduction sets a path for a refused essential condition, such as Standard 8.2's yearly talk on resource sufficiency. Luca has done the must, showing examples of the harm, and the should, offering alternatives. As Luca rejects the committee's reasons, those reasons should now be written down, shared with the board and senior management, and kept for the external assessor. Recording an agreed substitute, the closest choice, needs an agreement that does not exist.

wrong_explanations.A: Showing the harm with examples is the must, and Luca has already done it. Repeating it adds nothing once the committee has heard and rejected the case.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: reasons plus compensating conditions must be documented when everyone agrees a condition is unnecessary. Luca rejects the committee's reasons, so that branch does not apply.
wrong_explanations.D: The Standards do bind internal auditors, not boards, but that does not end Luca's part: the disagreement should still be written down, shared and kept for the external assessor.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the examples have already been shown and rejected, and D, because a board's freedom from requirements does not end the chief audit executive's part in documenting the disagreement.
Final two: C beats B because documenting reasons with a substitute fits only when everyone agrees the condition is unnecessary; Luca disagrees, so the disagreement itself is recorded and shared.
Exam cue: for a refused essential condition, follow the stage: show the harm with examples, offer alternatives, then document either the agreed substitute or the unresolved disagreement.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A topic the board adds in the charter discussion
questions.question: Discussing the proposed charter, a Luxembourg fund administrator's audit committee asks chief audit executive Claire to add how disagreements with management are handled, which the methodologies already set out. What is Claire's BEST response?

options.A: Leave it out, and raise it at the charter's next scheduled review
options.B: Add it, as the board may ask for topics beyond the minimum
options.C: Keep it in the methodologies, which the chief audit executive sets
options.D: Add it, as the Standards list it among a charter's required contents

questions.key_concept: The required charter content is a minimum. In discussing the proposed charter, the board may raise other topics, such as disagreement handling, for inclusion.
questions.pre_read: Standard 6.2 lists what every charter must contain. Is that list a minimum or a limit?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 sets the least a charter must hold, and its essential conditions have the board discuss other topics the charter should cover; its considerations name how disagreements with management are handled. Standards 13.1 and 14.4 separately require a methodology for disagreements, which Claire already has. Keeping the matter only in the methodologies, the closest choice, would refuse the approving body a clause the Standards invite it to request.

wrong_explanations.A: The Standards have the board raise other charter topics while the proposed charter is discussed, which is now. Deferring the clause its approver wants has no basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standards 13.1 and 14.4 do require a methodology for disagreements, and one exists. But the board approves the charter and may ask for more in it.
wrong_explanations.D: The Standards require a methodology for disagreements, not a charter clause. The clause belongs in this charter because the approving board asks for it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the charter is still under discussion and its approver wants the clause now, and D, because the Standards require a disagreement methodology, not a charter clause.
Final two: B beats C because the board, which approves the charter, may ask for topics beyond the minimum; the methodology Standards 13.1 and 14.4 require sits beside that clause, not in its place.
Exam cue: required charter content is a floor, not a ceiling. When the board asks for an extra topic while the charter is being discussed, the usual answer is to include it.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. Full-population testing and absolute assurance
questions.question: Internal auditor Mariama's analytics tested every claim a Guinean health insurer paid in 2025, and the audit committee asks whether that gives absolute assurance no improper claim was paid. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: No: assurance raises confidence, and no level of it is a guarantee
options.B: Yes: testing every claim removes the risk of a missed error
options.C: No: an internal audit engagement can give limited assurance at most
options.D: Yes, for 2025, if the claims data was complete and accurate

questions.key_concept: Testing a whole population still gives assurance, not a guarantee. The Standards name only limited and reasonable assurance, and neither is absolute.
questions.pre_read: Analytics can now test every transaction. Does testing everything change what assurance can promise?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary calls assurance a statement meant to raise stakeholders' confidence and lets internal auditors give either limited or reasonable assurance, with the level set by the kind, timing and amount of the procedures. Neither is a guarantee: testing every claim removes sampling risk but not, say, wrong source data or collusion, and Principle 4 says auditors are not expected to be infallible. The closest choice fails because internal auditors may give either level.

wrong_explanations.B: Full-population testing removes sampling risk, but the work still rests on the data and the tests chosen. Assurance raises confidence; it never promises that nothing was missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it rightly refuses a guarantee, but the glossary lets internal auditors give limited or reasonable assurance, the level following the procedures performed.
wrong_explanations.D: Complete, accurate data removes one gap, but judgment, collusion and the tests chosen still leave room for a miss. Assurance raises confidence; it never becomes a guarantee.

tips: Eliminate: B, because testing every item removes sampling risk but not every risk of a miss, and D, because even complete, accurate data leaves judgment and collusion, so no guarantee follows.
Final two: A beats C because both refuse a guarantee, but internal auditors may give limited or reasonable assurance; the level follows the procedures, with no cap set for internal audit.
Exam cue: absolute assurance is never on offer, however much is tested. When an option caps the level internal audit can give, check it against the procedures performed.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. Forensic support for legal counsel
questions.question: A Kuwaiti bank's legal counsel asks internal audit to trace and schedule payment records for a fraud claim the bank is bringing in court. How should internal auditor Dana BEST classify the service?

options.A: Assurance: the analysis compares the payments with set criteria
options.B: Advisory: internal audit alone sets its nature and scope
options.C: Advisory: it is forensic support given without an assurance conclusion
options.D: A role beyond internal auditing, needing safeguards in the charter

questions.key_concept: The glossary names forensic services as an example of advisory services: analysis and advice given without assurance or management responsibility.
questions.pre_read: Fraud work sounds like auditing against rules. Where does the Standards' glossary place forensic services?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary defines advisory services as advice that gives no assurance and takes on no management responsibility, and lists forensic services among its examples. Analyzing records for counsel's case gives no conclusion on governance, risk management or control, so it is advisory, with nature and scope agreed with the party that asked. Calling it assurance, the closest choice, mistakes comparing records for an objective assessment that ends in a conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: comparing records looks like testing, but assurance ends in a conclusion on processes. Analysis for a legal claim is forensic work, one of the glossary's advisory examples.
wrong_explanations.B: It is advisory, but the nature and scope of advisory work are agreed with the party requesting it, here legal counsel, not set by internal audit alone.
wrong_explanations.D: A role beyond internal auditing is a management duty the chief audit executive holds, such as running compliance. A single forensic engagement is an internal audit service.

tips: Eliminate: B, because advisory scope is agreed with the requesting party, not set by internal audit alone, and D, because one forensic engagement is an internal audit service, not a management role.
Final two: C beats A because assurance ends in a conclusion on governance, risk management or control; analysis for counsel's case gives none, and the glossary lists forensic services as advisory.
Exam cue: classify by what the work delivers. A conclusion that raises confidence in processes is assurance; analysis or advice for someone else's decision, forensic support included, is advisory.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A subsidiary head barred from local management
questions.question: A South Korean shipbuilder's group chief audit executive, Min-jun, bars the head of internal audit at its Vietnamese subsidiary from discussing any finding with that subsidiary's chief executive, citing independence. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: Sound: routing results through the group keeps the subsidiary unit independent
options.B: Unsound: subsidiary heads should be able to speak with local management directly
options.C: Unsound: the subsidiary head should report functionally to that chief executive
options.D: Sound: the group chief audit executive decides who receives results

questions.key_concept: Independence is not isolation: heads of internal audit in subsidiaries or divisions should be able to talk directly with the senior management of their units.
questions.pre_read: A group function protects its independence through its line to the board. Does that mean keeping subsidiary management at arm's length?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1's considerations expect heads of internal audit in subsidiaries, branches and divisions to be able to speak directly with the senior managers of those units, and Standard 13.1 requires internal auditors to communicate with management throughout an engagement. Min-jun may decide who receives final communications, but independence comes from the line to the board, not from silence. Routing everything through the group, the closest choice, mistakes isolation for independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independence rests on the functional line to the board and freedom from interference. Barring talks with local management adds isolation, not independence.
wrong_explanations.C: The functional line runs to the board, not to a chief executive. Direct talks with the subsidiary's management concern communication, not where the head reports.
wrong_explanations.D: Min-jun does decide who receives final communications, but that does not stretch to barring all talks with local management, which Standard 13.1 and the considerations expect.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the functional line runs to the board, never to a chief executive, and D, because deciding who receives final communications does not extend to barring all talks with management.
Final two: B beats A because independence comes from the reporting line and freedom from interference; the considerations want subsidiary heads able to speak directly with their units' managers.
Exam cue: independence is a matter of position and freedom from interference, never of silence. An option that cuts internal audit off from management in the name of independence is usually wrong.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. Filling a vacant chief audit executive post
questions.question: A Salvadoran coffee exporter's chief audit executive resigns without notice, and the chief financial officer, the administrative line, offers to run internal audit until a successor starts. Which arrangement is BEST?

options.A: The board itself names who leads internal audit in the meantime
options.B: The chief financial officer leads it, reporting to the board meanwhile
options.C: The most senior internal auditor takes over until a successor starts
options.D: Senior management names an acting head and informs the board

questions.key_concept: If the chief audit executive post falls vacant, the board should appoint one or more interim people; management does not fill it.
questions.pre_read: The board authorizes the chief audit executive's appointment. Does that change when the post is suddenly empty?
questions.correct_explanation: Domain III's introduction says that when the chief audit executive post is empty for any reason, the board should choose who acts until it is filled, matching its essential condition in Standard 7.1 to authorize appointment and removal. Promoting the senior auditor by seniority alone, the closest choice, skips the board's decision; a chief financial officer in charge would put management over the work that assures it.

wrong_explanations.B: A line to the board does not cure it: the board names the interim, and a chief financial officer in charge puts management over work that assures its areas.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a senior internal auditor may well be the right interim choice, but the board makes it. Seniority does not hand over the role by itself.
wrong_explanations.D: Senior management gives input on appointing the chief audit executive; the board authorizes it. An acting head chosen by management and reported later reverses that order.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a line to the board does not stop a chief financial officer in charge from directing assurance over finance, and D, because senior management gives input while the board authorizes the appointment.
Final two: A beats C because the right interim head may be the senior auditor, but the board names whoever acts; the role does not pass by seniority alone.
Exam cue: a vacancy does not move the board's powers. Whoever would appoint or remove the chief audit executive also decides who stands in meanwhile.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Who defines roles across the lines
questions.question: An Azerbaijani bank's audit committee wants chief audit executive Leyla, as integrator of assurance, to set the roles of risk, compliance and internal audit. Under current Three Lines guidance, who should MOST appropriately set them?

options.A: The board and Leyla, as internal audit integrates assurance
options.B: Senior management alone, as it designs the organization's structures
options.C: Each function's head, for the work that function performs
options.D: The board and senior management, above the three functions

questions.key_concept: The board and senior management define roles. Internal audit coordinates assurance but does not allocate roles, and its own mandate comes from the board.
questions.pre_read: The 2026 Three Lines statement calls internal audit an integrator of assurance. Does integrating mean deciding who does what?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement has the board and senior management set accountability by deciding who is responsible for what, and casts internal audit as an integrator that coordinates assurance without owning second-line work. Senior management alone, the closest choice, does design the structures, but internal audit's role comes from its mandate, which the board establishes under Principle 6. Leyla may advise; the decision is theirs.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit coordinates assurance providers and may advise on roles, but deciding roles, its own included, is not its job. Setting them would undermine its independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: senior management designs structures and creates second-line roles, but internal audit's role comes from the mandate the board establishes, so the board takes part.
wrong_explanations.C: Each head runs the work inside a function, but someone above the functions decides who does what across them. That is the board with senior management.

tips: Eliminate: A, because internal audit coordinates and advises but does not decide roles, its own included, and C, because roles across functions are set above the functions, not by each head.
Final two: D beats B because senior management designs the structures, but internal audit's role comes from a mandate the board establishes, so the two define accountability together.

Exam cue: integrator of assurance means coordinating and reporting a combined view, never assigning other functions' duties. Who does what across the lines is decided by the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. Direction from an official outside the oversight line
questions.question: A council member of a Brazilian city, outside the audit committee that oversees internal audit, tells chief audit executive Renata to audit a contract a rival council member approved. What should Renata do FIRST?

options.A: Start a short preliminary review to judge whether an audit is warranted
options.B: Consult the audit committee and senior management before acting on it
options.C: Add it to the plan, as elected officials speak for the public
options.D: Decline it, and note it in the audit committee's yearly confirmation

questions.key_concept: Public sector: before acting on an elected official without oversight of internal audit, the chief audit executive should consult the board and senior management.
questions.pre_read: Public-sector internal auditors hear from many elected officials. Who may direct the function's work, and what happens to a request from anyone else?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' public-sector section says a chief audit executive should hold back from an elected official's instructions until the bodies overseeing internal audit, the board and senior management, have been consulted; an official with an oversight role is the exception. This council member has none, and Standard 9.4 leaves the plan and significant changes to it for the board to approve. A preliminary review, the closest choice, already acts before that consultation.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: judging whether work is warranted is sound planning, but starting it here acts on an outside official's direction before the bodies that oversee internal audit are consulted.
wrong_explanations.C: Public input may inform the plan, but an official with no oversight role cannot direct it; the board approves the plan and significant changes to it.
wrong_explanations.D: Declining at once settles the request alone, before the consultation the public-sector section expects. Whether the episode belongs in the yearly independence confirmation is a later judgment.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the board, not any official, approves significant changes to the plan, and D, because declining at once skips the consultation that should come first.
Final two: B beats A because even a preliminary review acts on the direction; with an official outside the oversight line, the board and senior management are consulted first.
Exam cue: when an elected official with no oversight of internal audit tries to direct its work, the chief audit executive should consult the board and senior management before acting.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. A management expectation that limits independence
questions.question: Discussing the proposed charter, the chief executive of a Thai logistics firm asks chief audit executive Ploy to add that management agrees the scope of every assurance engagement. What is Ploy's BEST response?

options.A: Add the clause, as management's expectations are considered for inclusion
options.B: Leave the clause out, as it would impair independence
options.C: Put the request to the board, with its effect on independence
options.D: Agree a narrower clause with the chief executive, then tell the board

questions.key_concept: Senior management's charter expectations are input for the board, which approves the charter. The chief audit executive passes them on with their effect.
questions.pre_read: Senior management takes part in the charter discussion. What happens to an expectation of management's that would weaken internal audit's independence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.2 has the chief audit executive discuss the proposed charter with the board and senior management, whose expectations are input for the board, which approves it. Letting management agree assurance scope cuts against the board's essential condition in Standard 7.1 that scope be set free of interference, so Ploy takes the request and its effect to the board. Leaving it out, the closest choice, decides it for the board.

wrong_explanations.A: Management's expectations are weighed, but the board decides what the charter says. A clause handing management control of assurance scope may impair independence, so the board should hear its effect.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the clause may well impair independence, but the board weighs management's input as the charter's approver. Dropping it on Ploy's judgment alone makes Ploy the decider.
wrong_explanations.D: Bargaining the clause down with the chief executive settles the charter outside the board, which approves it. The board, not management, decides how far management's wishes go.

tips: Eliminate: A, because expectations are considered, not automatically adopted, and this one would let management steer assurance scope, and D, because the charter is settled by the board, not bargained with management.

Final two: C beats B because, however clear the threat to independence, the board that approves the charter weighs management's input; the chief audit executive explains the effect and does not decide alone.

Exam cue: in charter questions, the chief audit executive drafts and discusses, senior management gives input, and the board decides; management's wishes reach the board, neither adopted nor dropped on the way.

questions.subtopic: 1A3 Internal audit charter requirements. Examples of evidence for the charter discussion
questions.question: Internal auditor Kojo finds no minutes of the session where a Ghanaian insurer's board and senior management discussed the charter before approval; its agenda, slides and attendance list exist. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.A: Conformance can still be shown, as examples of evidence are not mandatory
options.B: Nonconformance, as board minutes are a listed example of evidence
options.C: Conformance is shown, since board approval implies the discussion took place
options.D: Nonconformance until the charter is discussed again and the session minuted

questions.key_concept: Each standard's examples of evidence are illustrations, not requirements, and not the only proof. Other records can show that a requirement was met.
questions.pre_read: Each standard ends with examples of evidence of conformance. Is every listed example a requirement in its own right?
questions.correct_explanation: Under the Fundamentals, each standard holds requirements (must), considerations (should or may) and a closing list of evidence examples. Those examples illustrate how conformance might be shown; they are not themselves required, and other records can serve. Standard 6.2 requires the charter discussion with the board and senior management, so the agenda, slides and attendance list can show it happened. Calling missing minutes a nonconformance, the closest choice, turns an illustration into a rule.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: minutes are among Standard 6.2's examples, but examples are not requirements. The requirement is the discussion, and other records can show it took place.
wrong_explanations.C: The verdict may hold, but not for that reason: approval shows the board voted, not that senior management took part in a discussion; the other records show that.
wrong_explanations.D: Repeating the discussion would fit if nothing showed it happened. Here other records do, so a fresh session adds nothing the requirement needs.

tips: Eliminate: C, because board approval does not show that the proposed charter was discussed with senior management, and D, because a repeat discussion is needed only when no record shows one happened.
Final two: A beats B because examples of evidence illustrate conformance and are not required; the requirement is the discussion, which other records can show.
Exam cue: read each part of a standard at its strength. Requirements say must, considerations say should or may, and examples of evidence only illustrate how conformance can be shown.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A scope limitation the board leaves standing
questions.question: A warehouse head withheld records from internal auditor Rosa's assurance engagement on a Kenyan brewer's four spare-parts warehouses; talks failed, and the board declined to intervene. How should Rosa's final communication BEST treat that warehouse?

options.A: Omit the warehouse, since the narrower scope is now settled
options.B: Hold the results and elevate the refusal to the board once more
options.C: Conclude on the warehouses examined; the board's minutes hold the reason
options.D: Explain the limitation, and conclude on the warehouses examined

questions.key_concept: An unresolved scope limitation is explained in the assurance final communication itself, and the conclusion covers only the work that could be done.
questions.pre_read: Once the board has heard of a scope limitation and chosen not to act, what does the limitation still change in the engagement's results?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 sends an unresolved scope limitation to the board, and the board's choice does not end Standard 15.1's requirement that the assurance final communication explain it to its readers. Standard 14.1 needs sufficient evidence for a conclusion, so it covers the three warehouses examined, and Rosa decides whether the withheld records are themselves a finding. Limiting the conclusion without the explanation, the closest choice, meets only half of that.

wrong_explanations.A: Nothing settled the scope: a board that declines to intervene leaves the limitation standing. Standard 15.1 still has the final communication explain it.
wrong_explanations.B: The board has already heard the matter and declined to act, so escalating again adds nothing. What remains is to issue results that explain the limitation.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the conclusion is rightly limited, but Standard 15.1 puts the explanation of a scope limitation in the final communication itself; board minutes do not reach its readers.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a board that declines to intervene leaves the limitation standing, not settled, and B, because the board has already heard it and the next step is the report.
Final two: D beats C because Standard 15.1 puts the explanation of a scope limitation in the final communication itself; a limited conclusion with the reason left in board minutes is incomplete.
Exam cue: a scope limitation changes results twice: the conclusion covers only what was examined, and the final communication says why. Escalating to the board replaces neither.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. Which budget arrangement restricts the work
questions.question: An audit committee member at a Croatian shipyard asks internal auditor Marija which of four budget arrangements could restrict internal audit's work. Which should Marija MOST clearly identify?

options.A: Internal audit's budget sits inside finance's, with its own share tracked
options.B: The board approved less than requested, though enough for the approved plan
options.C: Staff are funded, though not the analytics tool the plan's tests need
options.D: The administrative line reviews the budget before the board approves it

questions.key_concept: A budget is a limit when it cannot fund the planned work, tools included; its location, or a cut that covers the plan, is not.
questions.pre_read: Budget questions tempt you to flag every cut or every link to finance. What actually makes a budget a limit on internal audit's work?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.1 has the budget cover what the function needs to deliver its strategy and plan, technology and tools included, and Standard 7.1's considerations call a budget that leaves the function unable to do its work an undue limitation. Funding staff but not a tool the planned tests need does that. A smaller budget than requested, the closest choice, restricts nothing while it still covers the approved plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 10.1's considerations allow for a budget held within a larger one; the chief audit executive should still know the share, track spending and watch its sufficiency, as here.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: receiving less than asked is not itself a restriction. Here the budget still funds the approved plan, while C leaves planned tests without a tool they need.
wrong_explanations.D: Administrative reporting commonly runs budget processes, as Standard 6.2's considerations note; the board still approves the budget, so this review restricts nothing by itself.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a budget may sit inside a larger one if internal audit tracks its share, and D, because administrative review before board approval is a normal budget process.
Final two: C beats B because the test is whether the planned work can be done; a cut that still funds the plan does not restrict it, a missing needed tool does.
Exam cue: judge a budget by whether it lets the function deliver its strategy and plan, tools and training included; where the money sits, or who handles paperwork, is not a limit by itself.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A reporting line set by law
questions.question: By provincial law, a Philippine province's internal audit unit sits in the finance department it audits, and chief audit executive Jose reports to its head. Which safeguard should Jose BEST propose?

options.A: An administrative line to the governor, the functional line staying in finance
options.B: An audit committee of public members, free of management, to oversee it
options.C: A charter amendment moving the unit into the governor's office
options.D: A yearly confirmation of independence from Jose to the finance head

questions.key_concept: Where law places internal audit under managers it audits, an audit committee of public members with no management role can supply the missing oversight.
questions.pre_read: Some public-sector laws fix internal audit low in the structure. When the reporting line cannot be changed, what can still protect independence?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 7.1 builds independence on a direct line to a board, free of the management being audited, and requires Jose to document what in the structure limits it and which safeguards could help. For structures like this, the Standards' public-sector section names one: an audit committee of public members with no management role, overseeing the unit. A line to the governor, the closest choice, still leaves the functional line inside finance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reporting administratively to the head of the organization is leading practice, but the functional line would still run to the finance head whose department is audited.
wrong_explanations.C: A board can set reporting lines in a charter where it holds that power, but here a law fixes the placement, and a charter cannot override the law.
wrong_explanations.D: The yearly confirmation of independence goes to the board, not to a manager, and confirming to the audited department's head protects nothing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a charter cannot override a law that fixes the unit's placement, and D, because the yearly independence confirmation goes to the board, not to the audited manager.
Final two: B beats A because the problem is the functional line, not the administrative one; an independent audit committee gives the oversight that a reporting line to finance cannot.
Exam cue: when a structure fixed by law blocks a direct line to an independent board, look for added independent oversight, documented with the structure's limits, not cosmetic line changes.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. A temporary risk role split at the decision line
questions.question: Until a Mongolian bank without a risk function hires a chief risk officer, its board asks chief audit executive Saraa to keep the risk register and choose responses to top risks. Which course is BEST?

options.A: Decline both, as second-line work would impair independence
options.B: Take on both, with outside assurance until 12 months after hand-back
options.C: Take on the register as advisory work, leaving responses to management
options.D: Run the register only, with outside assurance and a hand-back plan

questions.key_concept: Internal audit may keep a second-line activity for a time, with safeguards. Choosing risk responses stays with management whatever safeguards are offered.
questions.pre_read: Some second-line work can be lent to internal audit with safeguards. Is there any risk task that no safeguard can make acceptable?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management says internal audit must not select or own risk responses, but accepts keeping a risk register as a temporary operating role with safeguards. Standard 7.1 sets those safeguards: an independent third party's assurance during the role and for 12 months after, and a plan to hand it back. Taking on both, the closest choice, stretches safeguards over a decision none can cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Second-line work is not barred outright: Standard 7.1 and the 2026 statement allow a temporary role with safeguards. Only the decision on responses is off limits.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside assurance for 12 months after hand-back is the right safeguard for the register, but the 2026 statement bars internal audit from selecting risk responses at all.
wrong_explanations.C: Keeping the register operates a management process, so it is a role beyond internal auditing needing safeguards, not advice. Facilitating a risk workshop would be advisory.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a temporary second-line role is allowed with safeguards, and C, because running the register is operating management's process, which needs safeguards, not an advisory label.
Final two: D beats B because safeguards can cover a temporary register role, but choosing risk responses is a management decision internal audit must not take, safeguards or not.
Exam cue: split a request at the decision line. Internal audit may advise, facilitate or temporarily run support work with safeguards; deciding how to respond to risk always stays with management.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A performance audit of a program's results
questions.question: Last quarter internal audit found a Portuguese hospital group's discharge reporting reliable; now its board wants assurance on whether a fast-discharge program delivers what it was launched for. Which engagement objective fits BEST?

options.A: Assess whether board reports compile the discharge figures accurately
options.B: Assess the program's results against peer hospitals' discharge times
options.C: Assess how far the program meets the targets management set for it
options.D: Assess whether discharges follow the health ministry's patient rules

questions.key_concept: A performance audit is an assurance service asking how well an activity or program achieves its goals, against adequate criteria such as management's own targets.
questions.pre_read: The board's question is about results. Which objective tells it how well the program is doing, rather than whether the figures are right?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary names operational or performance engagements among assurance services, and Standard 6.1's considerations give performance auditing as a service a mandate may name. The board asks how far the program meets its goals, and Standard 13.4 requires internal auditors to use adequate criteria the board and senior management have set, which program targets can be. Peer hospitals' times, the closest choice, would replace adequate criteria and answer a different question.

wrong_explanations.A: The reporting process was found reliable last quarter, so this would repeat that work. An audit of management reporting checks the figures, not whether the program achieves its goals.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: peer data can serve as criteria when management's are inadequate. Here management set targets, and Standard 13.4 requires adequate criteria already set to be used.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing against a ministry rule would be a compliance audit, which checks adherence to a requirement. The board asked about the program's results, not about following rules.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the reporting process was already found reliable, and D, because testing adherence to ministry rules is compliance work, not the results the board asked about.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 13.4 has internal auditors use adequate criteria management has set; peer times would only step in if the program's own targets were inadequate.
Exam cue: name an assurance engagement by the question it answers. 'How well is it achieving its goals?' is performance; 'are the reported figures right?' is management reporting.
