questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A quality audit beside a quality team's own checks
questions.question: A Turkish yogurt maker's quality assurance team, under the operations director, monitors the plants' quality checks, and the audit committee asks internal audit for a quality audit. How should internal auditor Emre BEST describe it?

options.A: Assurance on the quality process, including the team's own checks
options.B: A second-line review, since quality monitoring is the quality team's job
options.C: Advisory work, with its scope agreed with the quality manager
options.D: Assurance that relies on the quality team's reports as they stand

questions.key_concept: A quality audit is an assurance service. Internal audit, as the third line, can assess the quality process, including the second-line quality team's own checks.
questions.pre_read: A quality team already checks the product. Is internal audit's quality audit the same kind of work, or work from a different line?
questions.correct_explanation: The Part 1 syllabus lists quality audits among the assurance services an internal audit function performs. Standard 9.5's considerations count quality assurance among internal providers that sit in or report to management, and The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model has the third line give independent assurance, the second line's work included. Calling it a second-line review, the closest choice, confuses internal audit's engagement with the quality team's own monitoring.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the quality team's monitoring is second-line work inside management. Internal audit's quality audit is third-line assurance over the process, that monitoring included.
wrong_explanations.C: Advisory work would suit a manager asking for help to improve the process. The audit committee asked for an audit: assurance, with scope set mainly by internal auditors.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 9.5 requires a documented basis for relying on another provider's work, and its considerations call for evaluating that work first. Reports taken as they stand have neither.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the audit committee asked for an audit, not advice to the quality manager, and D, because relying on the team's reports needs a documented basis and an evaluation first.
Final two: A beats B because the quality team's checks are second-line monitoring; internal audit's quality audit is third-line assurance that can cover those very checks.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, an audit of quality, performance or culture by internal audit is third-line assurance, even where a management team already monitors the same area.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Recognizing advisory work on data privacy
questions.question: A Peruvian clinic chain's charter covers assurance and advisory services. Which request would MOST clearly make internal auditor Inés's work an advisory service on data privacy?

options.A: The audit committee asks whether consent records meet the privacy law
options.B: The privacy officer wants comments on how a new app collects consent
options.C: The privacy officer asks internal audit to run the monthly access reviews
options.D: The privacy officer wants comments confirming current consents meet the law

questions.key_concept: On data privacy, the internal auditor's advisory role is advice on privacy risks and planned controls, giving no conclusion; management owns the privacy program.
questions.pre_read: Who asks does not decide the kind of service. Look for advice without a conclusion and without running management's privacy controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The Part 1 syllabus lists data privacy among the advisory services internal auditors perform, and the glossary defines advisory services as advice given without assurance and without management responsibilities, such as advice on the design of new processes. Comments on how a new app collects consent fit that. Comments confirming that current consents meet the law, the closest choice, carry a conclusion against criteria, so they are assurance in all but name.

wrong_explanations.A: Whether consent records meet the law is a conclusion against criteria for the audit committee: a privacy audit, which is an assurance service, not advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Running access reviews operates a privacy control, which is management's responsibility. Advisory work can comment on how the reviews are designed, but never runs them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it is called comments and comes from management, but confirming that consents meet the law is a conclusion against criteria. That is assurance under another name.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a conclusion for the audit committee on meeting the law is a privacy audit, and C, because running access reviews operates a control that management owns.
Final two: B beats D because comments on a planned process give advice with no conclusion; comments confirming that consents meet the law conclude on compliance, which is assurance.
Exam cue: classify privacy work by its output. Advice on risks and planned controls is advisory; a conclusion on compliance is assurance; operating a privacy control is management's job.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. A request to write controls during training
questions.question: During risk and control training that internal auditor Tomás gives a Chilean winery's branch managers, one manager asks Tomás to write the branch's cash-handling procedures, to issue unchanged. What is Tomás's BEST response?

options.A: Explain the principles, and comment on a draft the manager writes
options.B: Write them, since the manager keeps the decision to issue them
options.C: Decline, as advice tailored to one branch would impair objectivity
options.D: Write them, and have another auditor review that branch later

questions.key_concept: In risk and control training the internal auditor explains and advises; management designs and owns its controls, even if it would adopt the auditor's text.
questions.pre_read: Training and advice are internal audit services. At what point does helping with a control become designing it?
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary lists training among advisory services, given without taking on management responsibilities, and The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement leaves designing and operating controls with management. Helping a manager design, by explaining principles and commenting on their draft, stays advice. Writing procedures the branch will issue unchanged, the closest choice, makes internal audit the designer; the 2026 risk statement likewise calls drafting policies a more operational role.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a manager issuing text unchanged has not designed it. The 2026 risk statement calls drafting policies a more operational role, which the board should approve, with safeguards.
wrong_explanations.C: Training and advice may address one branch's own risks. Objectivity is kept by leaving the design to management, not by refusing to discuss the branch's situation.
wrong_explanations.D: A later reviewer manages objectivity for the next audit, but does not turn writing the branch's controls into advice; that is an operating role the board should approve.

tips: Eliminate: C, because advice tailored to one branch is still advice, and D, because a later reviewer manages objectivity but does not turn writing the controls into advice.
Final two: A beats B because commenting on a manager's draft helps management design; writing text the branch issues unchanged makes internal audit the control's designer.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, the internal auditor teaches, comments and challenges; management writes, approves and runs its controls. Drafting them for management is an operating role, not advice, whoever signs.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Using a facilitated self-assessment in later assurance
questions.question: In March internal audit facilitated a Tunisian phosphate miner's shipping control self-assessment; the chief audit executive has confirmed this does not impair October's shipping assurance engagement. How should that engagement BEST use the team's ratings?

options.A: As internal audit's own evidence, since internal audit ran the workshop
options.B: As management's information, relied on once the auditors have checked it
options.C: Set aside, since a self-assessment is first-line work
options.D: As management's information, relied on where the team rated controls strong

questions.key_concept: Ratings from a self-assessment internal audit facilitated are management's own information; a later assurance engagement may use them only after evaluating their reliability.
questions.pre_read: Internal audit ran the workshop, but who produced the ratings? What does that make them in a later engagement?
questions.correct_explanation: In a facilitated self-assessment, managers rate their own risks and controls, so the ratings are management's information, not internal audit's findings. Standard 14.1 requires internal auditors to evaluate whether information is reliable, and reliability is stronger when the auditors obtain information directly or corroborate it. Treating the ratings as internal audit's own evidence, the closest choice, mistakes guiding the workshop for doing the assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: facilitating made internal audit the guide, not the assessor. The ratings are the team's own judgments, so they need testing before they support a conclusion.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's own information can be used once evaluated; nothing bars it. Setting the ratings aside fits only after testing shows they cannot be relied on.
wrong_explanations.D: A strong self-rating is the team's own view of its controls. Standard 14.1 requires the auditors to evaluate its reliability, so it cannot decide reliance by itself.

tips: Eliminate: C, because management's information may be used once evaluated, and D, because a team's strong rating of its own controls is the very information that needs checking.
Final two: B beats A because the team, not internal audit, produced the ratings; Standard 14.1 requires the auditors to evaluate their reliability before relying on them.
Exam cue: facilitating is not assessing. When a later engagement meets results internal audit only guided, treat them as management's information and test them before use.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. Assurance on a unit after advising on its due diligence
questions.question: Internal auditor Mei advised a Malaysian palm-oil group in due diligence on a target; four months after the purchase, the plan includes assurance on that unit. What is MOST clearly required before Mei joins?

options.A: Twelve months pass from the date the purchase was completed
options.B: The board approves the engagement as a significant plan change
options.C: An independent party outside internal audit oversees the engagement
options.D: The chief audit executive judges that the advice leaves objectivity intact

questions.key_concept: Assurance may follow advisory work in the same area once the chief audit executive confirms the advice does not impair objectivity and staffs accordingly.
questions.pre_read: The 12-month presumption concerns activities an auditor was responsible for. Did giving advice in due diligence make Mei responsible for the unit?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 2.2 allows assurance in an area internal audit earlier advised on, once the chief audit executive confirms the advice given has not compromised objectivity and staffs the work so each auditor stays objective. The Part 1 syllabus lists due diligence as advisory work. Waiting 12 months, the closest choice, borrows the presumption for an activity an auditor was responsible for, which advising is not.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the 12-month presumption covers an activity the auditor was responsible for. Advising in due diligence gave Mei no responsibility for the unit, so Standard 2.2's advisory rule applies.
wrong_explanations.B: The engagement is already in the plan, so no plan change arises. The board approves the plan and significant changes to it, not each staffing choice within it.
wrong_explanations.C: Oversight by an independent party outside internal audit is required when the chief audit executive is responsible for the function under review. Earlier advice does not call for it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the engagement is already in the plan, and C, because outside oversight is for functions the chief audit executive runs, not for earlier advice.
Final two: D beats A because giving advice is not being responsible for the unit; Standard 2.2 lets assurance follow advice once the chief audit executive confirms objectivity holds.
Exam cue: two rules follow earlier work. Past responsibility for an activity brings the 12-month presumption; past advice on it needs the chief audit executive's confirmation and suitable staffing.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 Kinds of assurance engagements. A contract audit with no right to audit
questions.question: A Colombian flower exporter's air-cargo contract has no right-to-audit clause, and the carrier refuses internal auditor Andrés its surcharge records for a contract compliance audit. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: A charter breach, as the access clause binds the carrier as well
options.B: A contract breach, to report as a finding against the carrier
options.C: A scope limitation, discussed with management and elevated if unresolved
options.D: No scope limitation, since the carrier sits outside the organization

questions.key_concept: Any condition that stops planned assurance work, an outside party's refusal included, is a scope limitation: discussed with management, raised with the board if unresolved.
questions.pre_read: The records sit with an outside party that never agreed to audits. Does that change what the refusal is, or only who can cure it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 defines a scope limitation as an assurance engagement condition, such as restricted access to data or information, that stops planned work. The carrier's refusal is one. It must be discussed with management, which holds the contract, and if it is not resolved the chief audit executive elevates it to the board. Treating it as no limitation, the closest choice, confuses whom the charter binds with what blocks the work.

wrong_explanations.A: The charter's access clause gives internal audit access within the organization, so it settles an employee's refusal. It cannot bind an outside carrier that never agreed to an audit.
wrong_explanations.B: Refusing records breaches the contract only if it grants a right to audit. Here the refusal limits the work, and Andrés decides whether missing evidence is itself a finding.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the charter cannot reach the carrier, but Standard 13.3 looks at what blocks the planned work, not at where the refusal comes from. The limitation stands.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the charter's access clause binds the organization, not an outside carrier, and B, because without a right-to-audit clause the refusal breaks no contract term.
Final two: C beats D because a scope limitation is whatever stops the planned work, whoever causes it; management is consulted first, and the board hears it if unresolved.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, judge a scope limitation by its effect on the planned work, not by who caused it. Then follow the order: management first, then the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. Where internal audit's authority comes from
questions.question: A Mexican furniture retailer's new chief executive tells chief audit executive Ximena that internal audit sees records only thanks to the chief executive's yearly memo to staff. Where does that access MOST accurately come from?

options.A: From senior management's support, which the yearly memo spreads
options.B: From its direct line to the board, as recorded in the charter
options.C: From the Standards, which every internal auditor has to follow
options.D: From Ximena's appointment, which the board itself authorized

questions.key_concept: Internal audit's authority, access to records included, comes from its direct line to the board, recorded in the approved charter; senior management promotes it.
questions.pre_read: Several parties help internal audit get access. Which one creates the authority, and which only supports it?
questions.correct_explanation: Internal audit's power to reach records rests on the board: Standard 6.1's considerations say the direct reporting line to the board is what creates the function's authority, and the board approves the charter recording the mandate. Senior management's essential condition there is to back the mandate across the organization and promote that authority. The memo, the closest choice, promotes the authority; it does not create it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: senior management is expected to support the mandate and promote internal audit's authority, and a memo does that. The authority itself is granted through the board.
wrong_explanations.C: The Standards set what internal auditors must do, and so shape the function's responsibilities. They give it no power inside an organization; the board and the charter do.
wrong_explanations.D: The board does authorize the chief audit executive's appointment, but that settles who leads the function. Access comes from the authority the direct line and the charter give it.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the Standards bind internal auditors but grant no power inside an organization, and D, because authorizing the appointment chooses who leads the function; it grants no access.
Final two: B beats A because the board creates the authority through the direct reporting line and the approved charter; senior management supports and promotes it.
Exam cue: separate who grants from who supports. The board grants authority and approves the charter; senior management gives input, then backs the mandate across the organization.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A proposed role beyond internal auditing
questions.question: The chief executive of a Ugandan bank proposes that chief audit executive Okello also lead a new compliance unit; the board has not yet considered it. What is MOST clearly required of Okello?

options.A: Accept, and report the role in the yearly independence confirmation
options.B: Accept once the chief executive agrees to outside assurance over it
options.C: Decline, telling the board and senior management it impairs independence
options.D: Discuss it with the board and senior management, advising on safeguards

questions.key_concept: A proposed role that could impair independence goes to the board and senior management for discussion, with the chief audit executive advising on safeguards.
questions.pre_read: The role is only proposed, and by management. Who must hear about it, and what must the chief audit executive bring to that discussion?
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 7.1, a role that could impair independence, whether held now or only proposed, must be talked through with the board and senior management, and the chief audit executive must advise both on safeguards. The board acknowledges the impairment when it approves such a role. Agreeing outside assurance with the chief executive, the closest choice, names a real safeguard but settles the role with management alone, before the board has weighed it.

wrong_explanations.A: The yearly confirmation reports incidents and the safeguards used, after the fact. A proposed role has to be discussed with the board and senior management before it is taken on.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside assurance is a real safeguard, but Standard 7.1 has Okello discuss the role with the board and senior management first; the chief executive cannot settle it alone.
wrong_explanations.C: The Standards allow roles beyond internal auditing, such as compliance, with safeguards. Even a role Okello doubts must first be discussed with the board and senior management, not refused alone.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the yearly confirmation reports after the fact, and C, because a compliance role is allowed with safeguards, so a flat refusal skips the required discussion.
Final two: D beats B because the board and senior management must discuss a proposed role and its safeguards; a safeguard agreed with the chief executive alone bypasses the board.
Exam cue: when a role beyond internal auditing is only proposed, the first duty is the discussion with the board and senior management. Safeguards come out of that discussion.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Owning management's external risk reporting
questions.question: An Indonesian cement maker's finance director asks chief audit executive Dewi to have internal audit write and file its stock exchange risk disclosures. Under The IIA's 2026 risk management statement, which response is BEST?

options.A: Hold it as an ongoing role, with safeguards in the charter
options.B: Hold it for a year, with outside assurance and a hand-back plan
options.C: Leave the disclosures to management, offering advice or assurance on them
options.D: Leave the disclosures to management, as external reports sit outside the charter

questions.key_concept: Under The IIA's 2026 risk management statement, internal audit must not own reporting to external parties; it may advise on or assure that reporting.
questions.pre_read: Some management work can be lent to internal audit with safeguards. Is reporting to outside parties one of those tasks?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 enterprise risk management statement says internal audit must not own reporting to external parties, while assurance over risk reporting, and advice on it, are part of its role. Writing and filing the disclosures would be owning them. Charter safeguards, the closest choice, are Standard 7.1's route for roles such as compliance; this task stays with management whatever the safeguards, though Dewi still discusses the request with the board and senior management.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 7.1's charter safeguards suit roles such as running compliance. The 2026 statement puts owning reporting to external parties among tasks internal audit must not take on.
wrong_explanations.B: The 2026 statement says a temporary assignment may soften the impact, which fits tasks such as keeping a register. Owning reporting to external parties is on its must-not list.
wrong_explanations.D: A charter covering the whole organization can reach external reporting processes, so internal audit may assure them. The disclosures stay with management because of ownership, not charter scope.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a temporary assignment softens only tasks internal audit may hold, not those on the statement's must-not list, and D, because the charter can reach external reporting; ownership is the issue.
Final two: C beats A because charter safeguards fit roles internal audit may hold, such as compliance; The IIA's 2026 statement keeps ownership of external reporting with management.

Exam cue: some tasks no safeguard covers. Under The IIA's 2026 statement, internal audit never owns risk responses, management's follow-up or external reporting; it advises or assures, and discusses the request with the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A fee cut to an outsourced internal audit function
questions.question: Mid-year, an Ecuadorian shrimp exporter's finance director cuts the outsourced internal audit firm's hours by a third, leaving the approved plan unmet. Which assessment by Paola, the firm's partner and chief audit executive, is BEST?

options.A: A budget limit to raise now with the board and senior management
options.B: A procurement change for management to settle with the firm
options.C: An impairment to report to the board in the yearly confirmation
options.D: A delivery shortfall for the firm to absorb under its contract

questions.key_concept: An outsourced function's fee is internal audit's budget; a cut leaving the plan unmet is a limitation the chief audit executive reports promptly.
questions.pre_read: The money goes to an outside firm under a supplier contract. Does that make the cut a purchasing matter, or still internal audit's budget?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 10.1 requires the chief audit executive to seek the board's approval of the budget and to tell the board and senior management promptly when financial resources fall short; its considerations add that the board should approve an adequate budget whether the function is insourced or outsourced. A cut that leaves the plan unmet restricts internal audit's work. Calling it procurement, the closest choice, hides a limit on the function from the board.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the firm is a supplier, but the Standards apply to contracted internal auditors too, so its fee is internal audit's budget, which the board approves.
wrong_explanations.C: The yearly confirmation does list incidents that may have impaired independence, but Standard 10.1 requires the impact of insufficient resources to be reported promptly, not months later.
wrong_explanations.D: A firm owes the hours its contract sets, but here the client cut them. The gap is the exporter's internal audit budget falling short, which the board must hear of.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the yearly confirmation comes too late for a shortfall that Standard 10.1 requires reported promptly, and D, because the shortfall comes from the client's cut, not the firm's delivery.
Final two: A beats B because an outsourced firm's fee is internal audit's budget; cutting it limits the board-approved plan, so its impact goes promptly to the board and senior management.
Exam cue: outsourcing changes who does the work, not the rules. Budget approval, and prompt news of any shortfall, still run to the board, whoever supplies the auditors.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Kinds of advisory work. A process map offered as grounds for reliance
questions.question: After internal auditor Wanjiku maps a Kenyan dairy's milk-collection process as advisory work, marking each quality check, the audit committee chair asks whether the committee can rely on those checks. Which reply is MOST accurate?

options.A: Yes, for design: the map shows a check wherever a risk arises
options.B: Not yet: the checks first need assurance work against criteria
options.C: Yes, once the collection manager signs the map as accurate
options.D: Not yet: the map first needs the chief audit executive's approval

questions.key_concept: A process map delivered as advice shows where controls sit; it gives no assurance. Reliance needs an assurance engagement that assesses them against criteria.
questions.pre_read: Drawing where a check sits is one thing; judging whether it would manage the risk is another. Which of the two did this work do?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary defines advisory services as advice given without providing assurance, and assurance as a statement that raises confidence by comparing the subject with established criteria. Wanjiku's map shows where the checks sit, but nobody has judged them against criteria. Calling the map assurance on design, the closest choice, mistakes locating a control for assessing it; an assurance engagement would have to make that assessment first.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a map shows where controls sit and helps later work. Judging whether their design manages the risk is an assessment against criteria, which advice does not give.
wrong_explanations.C: A manager's sign-off confirms that the map describes the process as it runs. It cannot turn a description into a conclusion on whether the checks work.
wrong_explanations.D: The chief audit executive approves an engagement's objectives, scope and final communication, but approval does not change the kind of service given. Advice stays advice.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a manager's sign-off confirms the map is accurate, not that the checks work, and D, because the chief audit executive's approval does not turn advice into assurance.
Final two: B beats A because showing where a check sits is description; judging whether it would manage the risk takes an assessment against criteria, which is assurance work.
Exam cue: ask what the work concluded. Advisory outputs such as maps and comparisons inform management; only an assessment against criteria lets the board rely on controls.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A request to shorten fieldwork
questions.question: At the start of a six-week assurance engagement on a Djiboutian port's crane maintenance, the maintenance head asks internal auditor Hodan to finish fieldwork in two weeks, citing peak season. What should Hodan do FIRST?

options.A: Accept two weeks, and explain the shorter fieldwork in the final communication
options.B: Report a scope limitation for the chief audit executive to elevate
options.C: Judge whether two weeks still leaves time for the approved work program
options.D: Judge whether peak season is a fair reason to shorten fieldwork

questions.key_concept: A request to shorten an assurance engagement may be a scope limitation: first judge whether it would stop the planned work.
questions.pre_read: Not every request from management limits the scope. What has to be true before this one counts as a scope limitation?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 treats a condition as a scope limitation when it blocks the planned work, its considerations ask auditors to weigh whether a restriction on an engagement's length is one, and Standard 13.5 requires them to consider the time frame. So Hodan first checks two weeks against the approved work program. Judging the peak-season reason, the closest choice, misses the test: a fair reason can still block the planned work.

wrong_explanations.A: The final communication must explain a scope limitation that stands, but accepting the cut skips weighing its effect and the discussion with management that Standard 13.3 requires.
wrong_explanations.B: An unresolved scope limitation does go to the board through the chief audit executive, but this request is not yet known to block the work, nor discussed with management.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: management's reasons deserve a hearing, but Standard 13.3 tests the effect: a restriction is a scope limitation if it blocks the planned work, whatever its reason.

tips: Eliminate: A, because accepting the cut skips weighing its effect and the talk with management, and B, because elevating comes only after a limitation is found and discussed with management.
Final two: C beats D because a restriction is a scope limitation when it blocks the planned work; whether management's reason is fair does not change that test.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, test a restriction against the work program, not against the reason given. If it blocks the planned work, it is a scope limitation: management first, then the board.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. A manager who sits in on every interview
questions.question: The approved work program for a Malagasy bottler's overtime assurance engagement calls for private interviews with staff, but the plant manager insists on attending each one. Which assessment by internal auditor Hery is MOST accurate?

options.A: A scope limitation, since it blocks the interviews the program planned
options.B: No scope limitation, since every interviewee in the program is still available
options.C: An objectivity concern for Hery to disclose to the engagement supervisor
options.D: A routine request to accept, as managers attend engagement meetings

questions.key_concept: Restricted access to personnel can also be a scope limitation: if it stops the work the program planned, it is one, though people stay available.
questions.pre_read: The staff are still there to talk to. What did the work program expect, and can it still be done?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.3 counts restricted access to personnel, not only to records, among the conditions that make a scope limitation when they stop the work the program expects. The program planned private interviews, and the manager's presence prevents them, so Hery has a scope limitation to discuss with management, which the chief audit executive elevates to the board if unresolved. The closest choice looks only at whether staff can be reached.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the staff can still be reached, but Standard 13.3 asks whether the planned work can be done. Interviews with the manager present are not the private ones planned.
wrong_explanations.C: Objectivity concerns Hery's own state of mind. Here management restricts access to people, which blocks planned work and, Standard 7.1 notes, can threaten the function's independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Engagements include opening and closing discussions with management. Sitting in on every staff interview is different: it restricts access to the people the program needs.

tips: Eliminate: C, because objectivity is about Hery's own judgment, not an obstacle placed on the work, and D, because sitting in on every interview goes beyond managers' usual part in an engagement.
Final two: A beats B because a scope limitation is judged by whether the planned work can be done, not by whether the people are still available.
Exam cue: restricted access covers people as well as records. If a condition stops what the work program set out to do, treat it as a scope limitation.

questions.subtopic: 1A7 Threats to internal audit independence. An officer who will filter findings
questions.question: Two months after chief audit executive Khamla's yearly independence confirmation, a Laotian airline's operations chief says they will decide which maintenance findings reach the audit committee from next quarter. Which step is MOST clearly required?

options.A: Disclose it to the board as an impairment of Khamla's objectivity
options.B: Report the potential impairment to the board and senior management
options.C: Hold it for the next yearly confirmation, with the actions taken
options.D: Ask the engagement team to disclose any objectivity concerns to Khamla

questions.key_concept: A potential impairment to independence goes to the board and senior management (Standard 8.1); the yearly confirmation reaches only the board.
questions.pre_read: Decide first whose independence or objectivity the plan touches, then which Standard says who must hear of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.1 requires the chief audit executive to report potential impairments to independence to the board and senior management, and its considerations favor timely word on significant issues. An operations chief choosing which findings reach the committee is the interference Standard 7.1 asks the board to prevent. Holding it for the yearly confirmation, the closest choice, reaches only the board, and only after the change takes effect next quarter.

wrong_explanations.A: An impairment of Khamla's own objectivity would go to the board, but nothing here biases Khamla. An officer filtering what reaches the committee threatens the function's independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: Standard 7.1's yearly confirmation must include such incidents, but it goes only to the board. Standard 8.1 also names senior management, and waiting misses next quarter's change.
wrong_explanations.D: Objectivity concerns an individual auditor's judgment. The threat here comes from the operations chief's control over results, which is the function's independence.

tips: Eliminate: A, because nothing here biases Khamla's own judgment, and D, because the threat comes from the operations chief's control over results, which is the function's independence.

Final two: B beats C because Standard 8.1 requires reporting potential impairments to both the board and senior management; the yearly confirmation reaches only the board, after the change takes effect.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, interference with what reaches the board is an independence matter, not an objectivity one. The chief audit executive usually reports it to the board and senior management promptly.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Writing management's risk report to the board
questions.question: A Fijian insurer's chief executive asks chief audit executive Mere to have internal audit write the enterprise risk report senior management gives the board. Under The IIA's 2026 risk statement, how is this BEST classified?

options.A: Its own administrative work, like consolidating risk reports with management
options.B: A task it must refuse, like owning reporting to external parties
options.C: An advisory service, safeguarded by agreeing its scope with the chief executive
options.D: A second-line role it may take on with board approval and safeguards

questions.key_concept: Preparing management's enterprise risk report stretches internal audit into a second-line role, allowed only with board approval and safeguards. Owning external reporting is barred outright.
questions.pre_read: The statement treats three reporting tasks differently: internal audit's own consolidation, management's report to the board, and reporting outside. Which is this?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management treats preparing enterprise risk reports on senior management's behalf as a broader, operating role that calls for safeguards such as board approval, charter documentation and independent assurance; Standard 7.1 adds that the chief audit executive discusses such a role with the board and senior management. Refusing it, the closest choice, stretches the statement's bar on owning reporting to external parties to a report that stays inside.

wrong_explanations.A: The statement treats consolidating risk reports with management as internal audit's own administrative work. Preparing the report on senior management's behalf is the broader role its Scenario A describes.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the 2026 statement bars internal audit from owning reporting to external parties. A report from senior management to the board stays inside; the statement allows it with safeguards.
wrong_explanations.C: Agreeing the scope fits advisory work, which gives advice without taking on management responsibility. Internal audit may advise on how clear the report is; writing it takes the task over.

tips: Eliminate: A, because consolidating risk reports with management is internal audit's own work, while writing management's report is not, and C, because writing the report takes the task over rather than advising on it.

Final two: D beats B because the statement's outright bar covers reporting to external parties; preparing management's internal risk report is a broader role allowed with board approval and safeguards.

Exam cue: sort risk reporting tasks three ways. Consolidating assurance results is internal audit's own work; management's internal report needs safeguards; reporting to outsiders is never internal audit's to own.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Performing finance's reconciliations
questions.question: With finance short-staffed, a Honduran bank's chief financial officer asks chief audit executive Iris to have internal audit perform finance's monthly suspense-account reconciliations, as its staff are independent of finance. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: A first-line control task that could impair internal audit's independence
options.B: An advisory service, as it gives finance practical help with its work
options.C: A second-line check that could impair internal audit's independence
options.D: An assurance service, as each reconciliation tests the accuracy of records

questions.key_concept: Performing a reconciliation is running a control: first-line work. Internal audit's independence is what that work could weaken, not a reason to take it on.
questions.pre_read: The chief financial officer cites independence. Place the task by what it is and who owns it, not by who is asked to do it.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 Three Lines statement places designing and operating controls with first-line management, back office included, and says a reviewer who operates a process cannot give credible assurance on it; Standard 7.1 has the chief audit executive raise roles that could impair independence with the board and senior management. A suspense-account reconciliation is finance's own control. Calling it second-line, the closest choice, mistakes who owns it.

wrong_explanations.B: Advisory work gives advice without taking on management responsibility. Performing the reconciliations is doing finance's work, not advising on it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: both lines' duties could impair independence, but second-line roles oversee risk in specialist areas. A reconciliation in finance's monthly close is finance's own control: first line.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives assurance by testing reconciliations that finance performs, against criteria. Performing them is the control itself, not an assessment of it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because advisory work never takes on management's tasks, and D, because assurance tests reconciliations finance performs; doing them is the control, not a test of it.
Final two: A beats C because a reconciliation in finance's monthly close is finance's own control, first-line work; second-line roles oversee risk in specialist areas such as compliance.
Exam cue: place the task by who owns it. Routine controls, back office included, are first line; specialist risk oversight is second line. Either, run by internal audit, could impair independence.

questions.subtopic: 1A8 Internal audit and the Three Lines Model. Seen as running risk management
questions.question: A Mauritanian telecom's internal audit only facilitates workshops and advises the new risk team, yet managers and an examiner say it runs risk management. Which safeguard should chief audit executive Sidi BEST propose?

options.A: Outside assurance over risk management for as long as it advises
options.B: An end to its advice, leaving workshops to the risk team
options.C: A written record of which line does each risk task
options.D: A note in the next yearly confirmation that no impairment exists

questions.key_concept: When internal audit only advises but seems to run risk management, the fitting safeguard is a documented split of roles that the board can see.
questions.pre_read: Internal audit operates nothing here. Is the problem a self-review threat, or a confused picture of who does what?
questions.correct_explanation: Both 2026 statements list a transparent, documented allocation of responsibilities, visible to the board, among the safeguards, and the risk management statement warns that unclear roles raise the risk of perceived impairment; Standard 7.1 has the chief audit executive advise on safeguards for perceived impairments too. Here internal audit operates nothing. Outside assurance, the closest choice, answers internal audit performing such work; it would not tell anyone who does what.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: independent assurance is the safeguard when internal audit performs or supervises risk management work. Here it only advises, and the confusion over roles would remain.
wrong_explanations.B: Advisory work on risk management is allowed and valuable. Stopping it treats a perception as a real overlap and still leaves the roles undefined.
wrong_explanations.D: The yearly confirmation is a duty, but a perceived impairment is addressed and made clear to the board when it arises, not just declared absent months later.

tips: Eliminate: B, because advising the risk team is allowed and stopping it leaves the roles undefined, and D, because declaring no impairment months later does not address a perception the board should hear of now.
Final two: C beats A because internal audit operates nothing here; outside assurance answers a self-review threat, while a documented split of roles answers confusion about who does what.
Exam cue: fit the safeguard to the threat. Performing second-line work calls for independent assurance over it; only appearing to calls for defined, documented roles that the board can see.

questions.subtopic: 1A2 The mandate and who sets it. A regulator's requirements placed in the mandate
questions.question: A Rwandan bank's regulator requires internal audit to report to the board quarterly and to conform with the Standards. Where in the mandate should chief audit executive Aline BEST place these?

options.A: In its role, recorded in the charter the board approves
options.B: In its authority, recorded in the charter the board approves
options.C: In its scope, recorded in the charter the board approves
options.D: In its responsibilities, recorded in the charter the board approves

questions.key_concept: The mandate's responsibilities are what the function answers for: carrying out its role, communicating, following laws and conforming with the Standards, plus stakeholders' specific expectations.
questions.pre_read: Role, authority and responsibilities sound alike. Which of them covers what the function is held to, rather than what it does or may reach?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 6.1's considerations treat responsibilities as what the function answers for in carrying out its role, plus what key stakeholders expect of it; communications, compliance with laws and conformance with the Standards are typical examples. A regulator's quarterly reporting rule and conformance duty belong there. The role, the closest choice, is what the function exists to do, chiefly delivering internal audit services, not the obligations attached.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the role is what the function is there to do, mainly deliver internal audit services. Duties to report and conform are obligations attached to that role.
wrong_explanations.B: Authority, created by the direct line to the board, opens access to the board, records, people and property. A duty to report quarterly is an obligation, not access.
wrong_explanations.C: Scope sets how much of the organization the services cover and which kinds are offered. It does not hold the duties attached to the work.

tips: Eliminate: B, because authority is the power of access that the board line creates, and C, because scope sets which areas and services are covered, not the duties attached to them.
Final two: D beats A because the role is what the function does, while duties to communicate, follow laws and conform with the Standards are the responsibilities attached to it.
Exam cue: in the mandate, authority is what internal audit may reach, the role is what it does, and responsibilities are what it answers for, stakeholders' expectations included.

questions.subtopic: 1A4 Assurance versus advisory services. A risk framework still in draft
questions.question: A Kyrgyz insurer's risk chief keeps reworking a draft framework that launches in three months; the board wants confidence by a regulator's review in ten months. Which plan should chief audit executive Aisuluu BEST propose?

options.A: Assure the draft's design now, and advise on any gaps found
options.B: Advise on the draft now, and assure it once in use
options.C: Build the risk register itself now, under outside assurance
options.D: Wait until the framework has run a year, then assure it

questions.key_concept: While a risk framework is still being built, advice usually helps most; assurance follows once it operates, staffed so earlier advice does not impair it.
questions.pre_read: Note what state the framework is in now and when the board needs confidence, then ask which service fits each point.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management says advisory support may be more prominent while risk management is still evolving, keeping independent assurance possible later. This draft keeps changing but launches well before the review, so advice now and assurance once it runs meet both needs; Standard 2.2 then has the chief audit executive confirm objectivity. Assuring the draft now, the closest choice, judges a document still being rewritten.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: assurance can cover design, but this draft is still changing, so a conclusion on it now would not hold for the framework the regulator will see.
wrong_explanations.C: The Three Lines statement lists a documented reason that the arrangement is necessary among its safeguards. A risk chief owns this framework, so the register is the second line's task.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting a year misses the regulator's review the board is preparing for, and gives up advice that could strengthen the framework while it is built.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a risk chief already owns the framework, so taking over the register is not necessary, and D, because waiting a year misses the review and forgoes advice while the framework is shaped.
Final two: B beats A because a draft still being reworked suits advice; assurance gives the board lasting confidence once the framework runs, three months in, well before the review.

Exam cue: on CIA questions, match the service to maturity. While a process is still being built, advice usually leads, keeping later assurance objective; once it runs and confidence is needed, assure.
